# CHAPTER 161

## THE PLAYER

Pell woke me by dropping the fish on my chest.

I made a noise that was not a word.

"It fell."

"From where?"

He pointed at the beam above us.

I looked up.

"Why was it there?"

"Drying."

"It's wood."

"Exactly."

I moved the fish onto his blanket.

It twitched once.

"Fuck you."

Pell was already pulling on his boots.

Morning had gotten into the stable loft through every crack in the
boards. Dust hung in the pale strips of light. Below us, something heavy
rolled across the carriage bay, stopped, rolled again, and Davin said a
word I couldn't hear.

Pell paused.

"That was bad."

"You heard the word?"

"No. Davin used one."

Fair.

My shoulders still knew about yesterday. My hands were better than they
had been after the northern shows. The skin at the base of my fingers
had stopped feeling newly offended by the crutches and settled into
ordinary complaint.

I checked my residual limb.

Fine.

I rewrapped it anyway.

Below us, Rinna shouted, "Breakfast before Marek finds it."

Pell was gone before I had my shirt buttoned.

That sounded less like urgency and more like experience.

Breakfast was in the service kitchen, not the dining room.

Good.

I did not want to meet thirty-five chairs again.

There were eggs, bread, porridge, two kinds of jam, apples, cold meat,
and enough butter that Marek had apparently decided it was a food.

He had three pieces of bread stacked in one hand.

Rinna took two away.

"Those are mine."

"They are breakfast."

"Yes."

"Eat breakfast."

"I am."

"Not tomorrow's."

Marek looked at the remaining bread in his hand.

"How do you know which is tomorrow's?"

Rinna pointed at the wrapped parcels stacked near the door.

"Because tomorrow's is wrapped."

Marek looked toward them.

Rinna said, "No."

He sat down.

I took eggs.

Private breakfast was better than public breakfast.

That was probably not a useful classification.

I kept it anyway.

Serra was already there, hair tied up, white flower gone from her coat.
She was writing something on a small piece of paper with the side of her
hand shielding it from Marek, who was not looking.

Or pretending not to.

Nessa drank something hot while staring at Pell's sleeve.

Pell noticed.

"What?"

"Turn."

He turned.

She reached across, pulled one loose thread free, and burned the end in
the candle.

"Done."

"Thank you."

"It was bothering me."

Orin came in last.

His bruise was darker.

Both shoes still matched.

Progress.

Marek pointed at him.

"Did you sleep?"

"No."

"Did you fight?"

"No."

"Did you win?"

"No."

Marek stopped.

"Interesting."

Orin took porridge.

Iven was irritatingly awake again.

"You're getting predictable," I told him.

"What?"

"Functional."

"Drink water."

"Fuck you."

"Also predictable."

Teren was not eating.

He had the folded paper from last night's bearded man open beside his
cup and another smaller note under it. Rinna sat opposite him with her
own piece of paper and a little stack of coins.

Not the whole company money.

Enough.

"Six days," Teren said.

"Five if Davin likes the south fork."

Davin came through the doorway carrying a metal ring the size of both my
hands.

"No."

Rinna looked at him.

"Five?"

"No."

"South fork?"

"No."

"Road?"

"Yes."

Teren folded the paper.

"Six."

Davin put the ring on the table.

Rinna picked it up, turned it over, and frowned.

"How much?"

"Seven."

"Copper?"

Davin looked offended.

"Silver?"

"Part."

I stopped eating.

Marek did too.

Rinna said, "How much part?"

Davin held two fingers about half an inch apart.

That did not help me.

It apparently helped Rinna.

She pushed one of the silver coins toward him, then held out her hand.

Davin took the silver and returned several copper from his pocket.

The metal ring disappeared into his coat.

Marek watched.

"What is it?"

"Wheel."

"Which part?"

Davin left.

Marek looked at me.

"Wheel."

"I heard."

"I understand wagons now."

"You should tell Davin."

"No."

Good.

Lady Merra never appeared.

Neither did Master Olan.

Harl did.

He came in while Marek was trying to wrap an egg in a napkin.

"No."

Marek froze.

Rinna looked delighted.

Harl pointed toward the carriage bay.

"Clear by nine."

Teren said, "We will."

"The east carriage leaves at half past."

"We'll be gone."

Harl looked at the wrapped food.

"All permitted?"

Rinna said, "Ask Mara."

"Which Mara?"

"The kitchen."

"We have three."

"The one who gave it to me."

Harl stared at her.

Rinna ate another spoonful of porridge.

Harl left.

I said, "Does anyone here have one name?"

Serra folded her note.

"Yes."

"Who?"

"No."

"That's Orin."

Orin lifted his spoon.

Breakfast ended because the wagons existed.

The company did not announce packing.

People simply started carrying things.

I had learned enough to finish eating first.

That felt important.

Then I carried my bag to the correct wagon.

Rinna watched me put it down.

"Good."

"I know."

"You want praise?"

"No."

"Good."

Pell handed me the fish.

"Why?"

"Hold."

"For how long?"

He was already gone.

I looked at the fish.

It looked back.

Painted eyes.

Still counts.

Nessa came through with two costume bundles and said, "Not there."

I moved.

"Where?"

"Anywhere else."

I moved again.

"Not there."

"You said anywhere."

"I was optimistic."

Eventually I ended up beside the rear wheel holding the fish, my own
bag, and a bundle of cloth that did not belong to me.

I did not know who had given me the cloth.

Serra passed.

"Useful."

"I have no idea what I'm doing."

"Also useful."

She put an apple on top of the cloth and left.

By the time Davin called for the wagon rail, the long box was already in
the carriage bay.

Upright.

Iron corners.

Dry.

Two stable hands helped him bring it out.

I watched the knot.

Then looked away.

Davin saw me.

"Good."

"I didn't do anything."

"Yes."

That was becoming insulting.

Teren came around the wagon with Harl.

"Nothing left?"

Harl asked.

Teren looked at Rinna.

Rinna looked at Nessa.

Nessa looked at Pell.

Pell looked at me.

I held up the fish.

"It's ours."

Pell nodded.

Harl said, "I don't want to know."

Correct.

We left at nine minutes after nine.

Harl looked at the sky as if those nine minutes belonged to him
personally.

No one from the family waved.

A kitchen woman did.

Serra waved back.

Maybe Mara.

Maybe not.

The estate disappeared behind walls and hedges faster than I expected.

Then we were on the east road.

Again.

Marek lasted twenty minutes before asking where we were going.

Teren was in the other wagon.

Rinna answered.

"East."

"I know that."

"Then why ask?"

"Specific east."

"Meal stop."

"Then?"

"Depends."

"On?"

"Money."

Marek sat up.

"Now we're talking."

Rinna ignored him.

The road was dry enough to be irritating rather than dangerous. Stone
appeared in stretches, then vanished under packed dirt, then returned
broken at the edges. Ditches ran beside us with expensive-looking
stonework full of weeds.

I had started recognizing bad roads by the way Davin's shoulders
changed.

He leaned before the wagon did.

Not always.

Enough.

Pell had the fish again.

It sat in his lap wrapped in cloth.

I asked, "What is that cloth?"

He looked down.

"Mine."

"Good."

I still did not know whose bundle I had carried.

Probably solved.

Serra sat opposite me with the note she had written at breakfast tucked
into her sleeve.

She looked out at fields.

A little after the first hour she said, "Stop."

Davin stopped.

No question.

Serra got down.

There was a stone post beside the road and a boy sitting on it with a
basket.

She gave him the folded note.

He gave her another.

No money that I saw.

No explanation.

She climbed back in.

Marek opened one eye.

"Romance?"

"No."

"Debt?"

"No."

"Crime?"

Serra looked at him.

"Sleep."

He did.

I wanted to ask who the note was for.

I didn't.

Progress.

At midday we reached a toll house where the road narrowed between two
stone posts and a chain.

I had seen tolls before.

I had not seen Rinna pay one for me.

The toll keeper came out with a board and counted horses, wagons, then
people.

"Players?"

Teren said, "Yes."

The man pointed at me.

"Him too?"

I looked behind myself.

There was nobody there.

Teren said, "Yes."

The keeper marked the board.

No one paused.

No one corrected.

Rinna handed over copper.

Not mine.

Company.

The chain came down.

We went through.

I thought about it for approximately the length of the gate.

Then Marek said, "How much?"

Rinna said, "No."

"I am asking academically."

"No."

"Professionally."

"No."

"Personally?"

"Especially no."

We stopped in a village an hour later.

I assumed we were staying.

I was wrong.

I discovered this after I had untied my bag.

Rinna looked at it on the ground.

"What are you doing?"

"Lodging."

"Food."

I looked at the inn.

"There's an inn."

"Yes."

"With rooms."

"Probably."

"We're not using them."

"No."

I retied my bag.

Marek watched from the doorway.

"Veteran."

"Fuck you."

"Passenger."

That was worse.

I hit him with the end of the strap.

The village had one main street, a smithy, a baker, a produce stall, two
chickens in a place chickens should not have been, and an inn whose sign
showed either a crown or a burning chair.

I was learning not to ask.

No one recognized us.

Excellent.

I went into the baker because Rinna gave me four copper and said, "Two
loaves. Dark. Not sweet."

I held the coins.

"For the company?"

She stared at me.

"No, Gregory. For a private bread collection."

"Right."

"Bring change."

That part felt more dangerous than Sword.

The baker was a woman with flour up both arms.

"Two dark loaves."

She pointed behind me.

I turned.

There were six.

"Which?"

"Dark."

"They're all dark."

She looked at me properly for the first time.

Then at my crutches.

Then past me toward the door.

"Move. You're blocking the onions."

I moved.

A boy carrying onions came through.

Good.

Yesterday I had been the expensive one.

Today I was in the way of onions.

Better.

The baker selected two loaves.

"Three copper."

I paid.

She gave one back.

I nearly put it in my own pocket.

Stopped.

Company change.

Rinna's.

I carried the bread out.

Marek intercepted me.

"Food."

"Company."

"I am company."

That was annoyingly difficult.

I held the bread higher.

"You can ask Rinna."

He went away.

Good.

Rinna took the loaves and the copper.

"You remembered."

"I almost didn't."

"Still remembered."

That was enough praise for the week.

We ate beside the inn.

Cold roast from Lady Merra's kitchen.

Bread we had just bought.

Cheese.

Apples.

The rich-house food tasted less rich beside a ditch.

Still good.

I bought a cup of hot broth from the inn for myself.

One copper.

I did it without asking the price twice.

That was new.

The woman handed it over.

I paid.

Done.

I had money.

Not much.

Enough that hot broth on a cool road did not require a meeting with
myself.

Marek watched.

"Buy me one."

"No."

"I spent my money."

"That sounds complete."

"Cards."

"Yes."

"And beer."

"Yes."

"And an investment."

I looked at him.

"What investment?"

He looked toward Orin.

Orin said, "No."

Marek sighed.

"Failed investment."

I drank my broth.

He did not get any.

Serra disappeared during the stop.

Not dramatically.

She walked down the side street and did not return for almost forty
minutes.

Teren noticed.

He asked Rinna, "Serra?"

"Back before wheels."

Apparently that was enough.

She returned before wheels carrying nothing.

A woman in a green apron walked with her as far as the corner, touched
her shoulder, then went back.

Serra climbed into the wagon.

Nobody asked.

Orin spent the entire stop sitting behind the inn with a man who had
come out of the kitchen.

They spoke quietly.

The man gave Orin a folded cloth packet.

Orin put it inside his coat.

Marek saw.

He opened his mouth.

I said, "No."

Marek looked at me.

"You're learning."

"I hate it."

"Good."

Teren and Rinna used the meal stop to argue about the next six days.

Not loudly.

Close enough that I heard pieces because I was sitting on the wagon
step.

The harvest fair was at a place called Dast.

Two days east if the road stayed good.

That confused me.

"Six days."

Teren looked at me.

"What?"

"The fair."

"In six."

"Dast is two days."

"Yes."

"So we get there four days early."

"No."

I waited.

He did not continue.

Rinna did.

"We don't go straight to Dast."

"Why?"

"Because four days early doesn't pay."

That made sense.

Mostly.

Teren tapped the folded paper against his knee.

There was a town southeast, half a day off the road, with a public hall
and no booking.

There was another east-road village with a yearly market in three days.

There was a mill settlement where someone owed Teren an answer.

There was also Carrow.

Not east.

I noticed that last part without anyone saying it.

Rinna said, "If Dast guarantees."

"They haven't."

"Then no."

"Gate plus floor."

"Not enough."

"Covered market."

"If it rains."

"Covered."

"If it sells."

Teren looked toward Marek.

Marek was trying to convince the innkeeper that actors required free
broth for cultural reasons.

The innkeeper was unconvinced.

Teren said, "We need one paid stop before Dast."

Rinna nodded.

"Two if Dast stays gate."

Davin came around the wagon.

"South road bad."

Teren looked up.

"How bad?"

Davin considered.

"Wheel."

Rinna said, "New?"

"No."

"Old?"

"Maybe."

Teren rubbed his face.

"East village?"

"Fine."

"Mill?"

Davin shrugged.

That was apparently a road report.

Teren folded the paper.

"East village tonight. Ask market in the morning."

Rinna said, "Lorn."

I had almost forgotten.

Not him.

Where he was.

Teren's face changed a little.

"Paid through tomorrow."

"After?"

"If he's still down, Bessa holds him another two nights. I left it."

"You told her?"

"Yes."

"Did he know?"

Teren paused.

"No."

Rinna stared.

"He was asleep."

"Still."

"I wrote it."

"To a sick man."

"He can read sick."

Marek had abandoned free broth and joined us.

"Who?"

"Lorn."

"Oh."

That was all.

Then, "Is he alive?"

Teren looked at him.

"Yes."

"Good."

Marek sat down.

I asked, "He catches us?"

"If he can," Teren said.

"How?"

"Coach, freight wagon, another company, walking if he wants to die."

"Does he know where we're going?"

Teren held up the paper.

"I don't know where we're going."

Fair.

Rinna said, "Bessa knows east road."

That was apparently enough for now.

The road started again.

East village tonight.

Not a show.

Maybe market work tomorrow.

Maybe Dast in six days.

Maybe something between.

I tried to count how many days I had been gone.

That went badly.

Carrow had become a sequence of mornings instead of a date.

Hessa had said next assessment when I returned.

Lyssa had said come back.

I had said I would.

None of those things had changed.

The road still went east.

I put my hand inside my coat and felt the scrap paper around the brass
clasp.

Still there.

My letter might reach Carrow tomorrow.

Or the next day.

Depending on road.

Depending on someone else's wagon.

Depending on weather.

Apparently everything depended on road.

Marek woke from his latest sleep.

"Where are we?"

"East."

He looked offended.

"Specific."

"Village tonight."

"Show?"

"No."

He frowned.

"Money?"

"No."

He lay back down.

"Wake me when capitalism returns."

I did not know the word.

Neither, apparently, did he.

I said, "What?"

He opened one eye.

"What?"

"You said something."

"No."

"You absolutely did."

"Sleep."

Serra laughed into her sleeve.

I decided not to pursue it.

The afternoon became fields.

Then woods.

Then fields again.

The road narrowed.

We passed a funeral going the other direction, six people walking behind
a cart with flowers on it. Everyone in our wagon stopped talking until
they passed.

No reason given.

Later we passed three boys driving pigs.

One pig escaped.

Iven got down to help because he was nearest.

The pig did not respect theatre.

It took eleven minutes.

When Iven came back muddy to the knee, Marek applauded.

Iven said, "I will kill you."

Marek said, "Strong second act."

Nobody paid us.

Near sunset, the east village appeared around a low stone bridge.

Not much of a village.

Maybe forty buildings.

Smoke.

A square.

A chapel.

A long inn with a stable yard.

Teren went inside before we unloaded anything.

Rinna said, "Wait."

So we waited.

This, too, I had learned.

Do not unload until someone has bought the right to make you unload.

Davin checked the new metal ring near the rear wheel.

Nessa took one costume bundle down because she said damp did not care
about contracts.

Pell gave me the fish.

I accepted it without asking why.

That was probably a mistake.

A girl crossed the square carrying a bucket.

She looked at the wagons.

Then at me.

Then at the fish.

"What's that?"

I looked down.

"Problem."

Pell, from under the wagon, said, "Prop."

The girl nodded as if that made more sense.

It probably did.

Teren came back out.

"Rooms are too much."

Marek groaned.

"Stable loft?"

"Full."

"Floor?"

"Also money."

Rinna asked, "Food?"

"Cheap enough."

"Sleep?"

Teren looked across the square.

There was a low warehouse beside the bridge.

"Merchant keeps freight there. Dry floor. One copper each."

Marek sat up.

"Each?"

"Company."

"Oh."

That changed his expression immediately.

Teren continued.

"No fire. No singing. Out by seven."

Orin said, "Good."

Marek said, "Bad."

Teren ignored both.

"Market master comes at breakfast. He may want something tomorrow."

"Paid?" Marek asked.

"Maybe."

"Wake me then."

Teren looked at me.

"Fish."

I looked at the thing in my hands.

"What?"

"Keep it with the props tonight."

That was all.

Not Pell.

Me.

I carried it across the square with the others.

Our props.

I did not notice the word until much later.

The warehouse smelled of rope, grain dust, old river water, and somebody
else's onions.

Of course onions.

Rinna paid the merchant from the company coins.

Davin chose the driest wall for the long box.

Upright.

Dry.

Unopened.

Nessa claimed a corner for costumes.

Pell immediately tried to put the fish beside my bedroll.

I moved it to the prop pile.

"Work."

He looked at me.

Then nodded.

Outside, Teren and Rinna were still talking about Dast.

Six days.

East.

Maybe.

I sat on my blanket and took off my boots.

For the first time since leaving Carrow, I understood that I did not
know when I was going back.

That should have frightened me more than it did.

Instead I was tired.

Hungry again.

Five copper for a public show.

Six for private.

Two more if a rich old man wanted seven minutes of regret.

One copper for hot broth.

Company copper for bread.

Company silver for wheels.

Free breakfast if somebody negotiated it.

A warehouse floor if rooms cost too much.

Tomorrow maybe work.

Maybe not.

I could go back.

Not tonight.

Probably not tomorrow.

I looked east through the open warehouse door while there was still
enough light to see the bridge.

Then Pell's fish twitched in the prop pile.

I said, "No."

Nobody asked why.

# CHAPTER 162

## THE STREET PLAYER

Someone kicked my boot before dawn.

I opened my eyes.

Nothing.

Then it happened again.

I sat up.

The fish was beside my foot.

Pell was asleep three blankets away.

I looked at the prop pile.

There was a fish-shaped absence.

"No."

The warehouse was almost dark. A gray line had appeared under the door,
enough to make the ropes hanging from the rafters look like bodies if I
was stupid.

I was tired enough to be stupid.

The fish twitched.

I picked it up by the tail.

"You're going back."

"Talking to props?"

Iven's voice came from the dark.

"No."

"Good."

"Why are you awake?"

"You're talking to a fish."

"That happened after."

"Still."

Somewhere near the wall Marek snored once, stopped, then resumed with
more confidence.

I carried the fish back to the prop pile and wedged it between the
battered Shopkeeper table leg and a basket of wooden cups.

It stayed.

For approximately six seconds.

Then Rinna said, "Up."

Nobody argued.

We had to be out by seven.

That turned out to be earlier than my body believed seven should be.

The warehouse became a machine in the dark. Blankets rolled. Bags
closed. Costume bundles appeared from Nessa's corner. Davin opened the
carriage door and let in cold air that smelled like river water and
horse.

Pell found the fish.

"Why is it there?"

"Props."

"It was by you."

"It moved."

Pell looked at me.

"Did you move it?"

"Yes."

"Then it didn't."

I hated him.

Outside, the village was already awake in pieces. A baker had smoke
coming from his chimney. Someone was dragging a cart across the bridge.
The chapel bell rang once, paused, then rang again as if reconsidering.

Davin and two men from somewhere I had not seen the night before moved
the long box out first.

Upright.

Dry.

Still closed.

I held the warehouse door because that was useful and because nobody had
asked me to carry the thing.

Davin glanced at me.

"Good."

"You're going to ruin that word."

He kept walking.

Rinna paid the merchant.

One copper each had sounded cheap until I watched her count enough coins
for all of us.

Then it looked like a meal.

Or two loaves.

Or several hot broths I was not buying Marek.

The merchant counted the coins twice.

"No fire?"

Rinna said, "No fire."

"No singing?"

Marek, carrying a blanket bundle, said, "Debatable."

The merchant looked at Teren.

Teren said, "No singing."

Marek looked betrayed.

"Out by seven?"

"We are leaving."

The merchant looked around the empty floor.

The only thing left was one onion near the wall.

He pointed.

"Yours?"

Teren looked at us.

Nobody claimed it.

Orin said, "No."

The merchant sighed.

We were out by seven.

Breakfast happened on the edge of the square because the market had
started arriving before we finished leaving the warehouse.

Rinna gave us bread, cheese ends, and apples.

Marek looked toward the wrapped roast.

Rinna said, "No."

"I didn't ask."

"You looked."

"I have eyes."

"Use them on the bread."

The roast stayed wrapped.

I ate bread.

The square changed while I was sitting there.

At first there were empty patches of packed dirt and stone. Then carts
arrived. A woman claimed half the chapel wall with baskets of onions.
Two men unfolded a cloth awning between poles. Someone backed a cart
full of cabbages directly into another cart and both drivers became
personally offended by geometry.

Chickens appeared.

Nobody brought them.

They were simply there.

A fish seller laid silver bodies over crushed ice in shallow wooden
trays. Smoke from a sausage pan moved low through the square. A boy with
three belts over one shoulder shouted prices at people who were not
listening.

By the time I finished my apple, the place had become difficult to
cross.

My crutches made it worse.

People saw one crutch and stepped around it, then nearly walked into the
other. I learned quickly that moving slowly did not make people patient.
It gave them more time to make bad decisions.

"Players?"

The voice came from behind me.

I turned.

A woman stood with Teren near the well.

She was perhaps fifty, maybe older, with a red wool cap pulled low over
gray hair and a leather ledger tucked under one arm. She wore an apron
with three pockets and had chalk on one sleeve.

Teren pointed at her.

"Market master."

She said, "Dema."

I said, "Gregory."

"I didn't ask."

"Good morning."

"Maybe."

I liked her less than Bessa.

Not in a bad way.

Dema looked across the square at the wagons.

"How many?"

Teren answered.

"Depends what you want."

"I asked how many people."

"Enough."

Dema stared at him.

Rinna came over carrying a cup.

"Twelve traveling. More or less working depending on what you're
counting."

Dema looked at her.

"Better."

Teren did not appear offended.

That was probably why Rinna was there.

Dema opened her ledger.

"I have vendors paying for a market. I have a cooper who says music
keeps people near his stall and a fish woman who says music keeps people
from buying fish."

"Does she sell bad fish?" Marek asked.

Dema looked past me.

Marek had appeared with bread.

"Who is that?"

Teren said, "Problem."

"Actor," Marek corrected.

"Same rate?"

"Usually higher."

Dema ignored him.

She wanted something from eleven until one.

Not a play.

Not even close.

"Noise," she said.

Teren said, "You can get noise free."

"I have noise."

She pointed at the square.

A man shouted, "TURNIPS!"

Dema waited.

"See?"

Teren nodded.

"What do you want?"

"People to stay."

"That's not a performance."

"Then perform something that makes them stay."

"How long?"

"Two hours."

Teren laughed.

Dema did not.

Rinna said, "Continuous?"

"No. I'm not cruel."

"How many sets?"

Dema thought.

"Three."

"Length?"

"Ten minutes."

"That's thirty minutes."

"I can count."

"Then why say eleven to one?"

"Because if you do all thirty at eleven, you're stupid."

Fair.

Teren asked, "What are you paying?"

Dema named a number.

I did not hear it because the sausage seller dropped a pan.

Rinna heard it.

Her face did not change.

Teren's did.

"No."

Dema closed the ledger.

"Good breakfast."

She turned away.

Marek said, "Wait."

Teren looked at him.

Marek stopped.

Rinna said, "Food?"

Dema turned back.

"What?"

"For the company. Midday."

Dema looked at the square.

"Vendors contribute."

"To what?"

"Food."

"Guaranteed?"

"Yes."

"How much cash?"

Dema named another number.

This one I heard.

It was not enough for a full show.

I knew that much now.

Teren said, "Plus hat."

Dema said, "No begging."

"Collection."

"No."

"Tips."

"No."

Marek whispered, "Tyrant."

Dema heard him.

"Especially no."

Teren said, "Two sets."

"Three."

"Eight minutes."

"Ten."

"Three sets, eight."

Dema shook her head.

"Three tens."

Rinna said, "Lunch for twelve."

Dema looked at her ledger.

"Ten."

"Twelve."

"Your man said twelve traveling."

"Exactly."

"Some of them can buy lunch."

Rinna smiled.

Not pleasantly.

Teren said, "Twelve."

Dema looked between them.

"Three sets. Ten minutes. No hat. Lunch for twelve. Twelve copper
company fee."

I knew that number.

Not because I knew company finance.

Because it was more than two loaves and less than a private house.

Teren said, "Fifteen."

Dema said, "Twelve."

"Fourteen."

"Twelve."

"Thirteen."

Dema opened her ledger.

"Twelve."

Teren held out his hand.

"Fine."

Dema shook it.

Marek said, "What do we get?"

Teren said, "Lunch."

"I mean money."

"Company gets twelve."

"I am company."

Rinna said, "You said that yesterday when stealing bread."

"I was right yesterday."

Teren looked at him.

"Three short sets. Nobody gets show rate."

I asked, "Do we get anything?"

Teren looked at me.

"One copper each for anyone in all three sets. Company keeps the rest."

Marek brightened.

"Work."

Rinna said, "You spent six yesterday."

"That was private Marek."

"What is this?"

"Market Marek."

Orin said, "Worse."

Dema had already walked away.

That was the booking.

If it counted as a booking.

Three ten-minute pieces over two hours.

Lunch.

One copper for me if I worked all three.

I had paid one copper for broth yesterday.

That was a strange way to understand wages.

Teren looked around.

"Nothing complicated."

Marek said, "Excellent."

"That's for you."

"Less excellent."

Teren pointed toward the square.

"First set there. Second near cloth row. Third back here."

I looked.

"There are carts there."

"Not at eleven."

"How do you know?"

"I don't."

Good.

He started assigning people.

Not roles.

People.

Marek, Serra, Iven, Orin, me.

Pell if needed.

Nessa said no before anyone asked.

Rinna definitely no.

Davin had already disappeared toward the wagons.

"What are we doing?" I asked.

Teren said, "Things people stop for."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the one you have."

Then he left to find Dema again.

Marek rubbed his hands.

"I have ideas."

Serra said, "No."

"I haven't said them."

"Good."

The first set became Sword because the board was portable and because
Marek could be loud.

That was the entire planning process.

Pell and I carried the mounting board toward the well.

Mostly Pell.

I held the fish.

"Why?"

"Opening."

"What opening?"

He kept walking.

I followed.

The square was worse now.

A woman carrying eggs told me to move.

A man carrying cloth told her to move.

A dog stood in the middle of both of them and refused government.

We found a patch beside the well.

Teren looked at it.

"No."

"Why?"

"Cart."

There was no cart.

Then a cart arrived.

Fine.

We moved six yards.

Iven used chalk to mark a rough edge.

Not a stage.

A warning.

"Don't go past that," he told me.

"Why?"

"Fish water."

I looked behind me.

The fish seller had a bucket draining across the stones.

Good.

I shifted right.

That put me near onions.

I was developing enemies.

The first set began because Marek climbed onto an empty crate and
shouted:

"WHO HERE CAN AFFORD A KING?"

People looked.

Not everyone.

Enough.

A cabbage seller shouted, "Not me."

Marek pointed at him.

"Then you may look for free."

That got a few laughs.

Serra walked into the space.

"Your Majesty, nobody asked for you."

"That has never stopped monarchy."

More people looked.

Pell shoved the fish into my lap and ran away.

I was mounted beside a well, three feet from onions, holding a wooden
fish.

This was not how Sword usually began.

Serra looked at me.

Then at the fish.

"What have you done?"

I said, "I found dinner."

The fish twitched.

A child screamed happily.

That helped.

Marek said, "That is not dinner. That is the royal beast."

I looked at the fish.

"It has poor breeding."

A fish seller shouted, "So do you!"

The crowd laughed harder at her.

Correctly.

I looked toward her.

"Madam, your relatives are on ice."

That got her.

She slapped the side of her table.

People stopped.

Not everyone.

A man bought onions during my next line.

Two women walked directly through the edge of the set because they
wanted cloth.

A dog smelled the mounting board.

Sword had never dealt with a dog.

Serra did.

"Don't."

The dog looked at her.

Then left.

I said, "Teach me that."

"You're worse."

The set lasted maybe nine minutes.

Maybe eleven.

I could not tell because market time had no walls.

People arrived halfway through.

People left before the end.

A man who laughed at one line never heard the next because someone
showed him a knife for sale.

When Teren clapped once, Marek ended.

Not with the planned ending.

I did not know there had been one.

Marek pointed at me.

"The sword is not for sale."

I said, "Everything is for sale."

Serra looked at me.

I added, "Apparently not here."

Teren said, "Done."

We stopped.

The crowd did not applaud as one thing.

Some people did.

Some immediately went back to buying.

One child asked Pell whether the fish was real.

Pell said, "Mostly."

I said, "No."

The child touched it.

It bit him.

Not hard.

He laughed.

Pell looked at me.

"See?"

"You said it didn't."

"When?"

"Several towns ago."

"Different fish."

I stared at him.

He took it away.

I believed nothing.

The second set was supposed to be Shopkeeper.

Then Dema moved us.

The cloth row had become too crowded.

She pointed toward the far end of the square beside a potter.

"Here."

Teren looked at the ground.

Mud.

He looked at me.

I looked at him.

"No."

Dema said, "Why?"

Teren pointed at my crutches.

Dema looked.

Then at the stones behind the potter.

"Move his table."

The potter said, "No."

Dema said, "You paid for six feet. You're using eight."

The potter moved his table.

I liked Dema more.

We got stone.

Shopkeeper started with Iven trying to cross the market carrying a
basket.

I stopped him.

"Pay me."

"For what?"

"Passage."

"This is a public road."

"Not anymore."

A vegetable seller said, "He's right."

I pointed at her.

"Thank you."

She said, "You owe me."

"Never mind."

That worked.

Then a customer asked Iven how much the basket cost.

He answered.

Actually answered.

The customer tried to buy it.

The basket was a prop.

Iven looked at Teren.

Teren looked away.

Iven said, "Three copper."

I said, "Five."

The customer said, "Two."

We had accidentally become merchants.

The crowd liked this more than the scene.

Iven said, "Four."

The customer said, "Two and an onion."

I said, "The onion is mine."

The onion seller shouted, "No it isn't!"

I said, "Debt."

That got enough people laughing that the customer realized something was
happening.

He did not buy the basket.

Good.

We found the scene again.

Mostly.

At one point a cart came through and we stopped.

Not theatrically.

We moved.

The horse did not care about pacing.

Once it passed, Iven said, "Where were we?"

I said, "You owed me money."

"That doesn't narrow it down."

Good.

We continued.

I was beginning to understand why Teren had said things people stop for.

Not scenes people watch.

Stopping was the first problem.

Then staying.

Then leaving before the horse.

Nobody explained this.

They were too busy avoiding the horse.

Between sets I was given an ordinary responsibility.

Rinna handed me two copper.

"Water."

"For?"

"Us."

"How much?"

"Cheapest clean."

That sounded like a trap.

I found a woman selling cups near the chapel.

One copper filled a small jug.

I bought two jugs.

No change.

I carried one awkwardly with a finger hooked through the handle while
using my crutches.

This was stupid.

I made it twelve steps.

Then a girl selling buttons said, "Give me that."

I did.

She carried both jugs to Rinna.

Rinna gave her an apple.

No money.

The girl left.

I said, "I could have done that."

Rinna said, "Badly."

"Yes."

"Then don't."

Useful.

Annoying.

The third set nearly did not happen.

At twelve forty-five Dema found Teren.

"Enough."

Teren said, "We owe three."

"You did two."

"We were hired for three."

"I know."

"Then?"

"Vendors are complaining."

"Which?"

She pointed.

Fish woman.

Potter.

A man selling ribbons.

The cabbage seller was not complaining.

He had apparently sold out.

Teren said, "We do the third quieter."

Dema looked at Marek.

"No."

Marek looked wounded.

Serra said, "We can."

Teren thought.

Then pointed at Orin.

"Death."

Orin said, "No."

"Short."

"No."

"Quiet."

Orin looked at the market.

Then at the fish woman.

"Fine."

I had never seen Orin's little death piece.

Apparently neither had half the company.

It required a stool, one cup, Orin, Serra, and almost nothing else.

I was not in it.

That meant no copper.

I looked at Teren.

He looked at me.

"You're in the end."

"What end?"

"You'll know."

I hated that.

The piece began almost quietly.

Orin sat with the cup.

Serra asked him why he had come.

He said he was waiting to die.

A woman buying ribbons slowed.

Then stopped.

The piece was funny.

Not loud funny.

Orin complained that death was late.

Serra suggested he had the wrong day.

Orin accused death of poor administration.

I almost said jurisdiction from the side.

I bit the inside of my cheek.

Good.

More people stopped because other people had stopped.

That was different.

No shouting.

No King.

No fish.

At the end Serra looked around as if searching.

"Perhaps death took someone else."

Teren pointed at me.

I understood nothing.

Then Orin looked directly at me.

"One leg."

Fuck him.

I entered.

"What?"

Orin said, "Did you see death?"

I looked behind myself.

"No."

"Then he took the other one."

The crowd made a sound.

Not huge.

Good.

I looked down at myself.

Then at Orin.

"Late."

Orin nodded.

"Always."

I said, "Charge him."

Orin handed me the cup.

"Your department."

Shopkeeper.

Fine.

I took the cup.

"Pay me."

That was the end.

People laughed.

Then the sausage seller shouted lunch.

The market broke apart.

Work ended.

No bow.

No curtain.

No doors closing.

Just food.

Dema found Teren near the well and counted twelve copper into his hand.

He counted.

Rinna watched.

Dema said, "Three sets."

Teren said, "Three."

"Third was better."

Marek, close enough to hear, said, "I wasn't in it."

Dema said, "Yes."

Marek looked at Serra.

"Hostile village."

Dema walked away.

Lunch came from vendors in pieces.

Bread from one.

Sausages from another.

Apples.

A pot of beans.

Cheese.

The fish woman sent nothing.

Fair.

Rinna made sure twelve people ate.

Davin appeared exactly when food did.

I had not seen him for two hours.

"Where were you?"

"Wagon."

"Doing what?"

"Wheel."

Of course.

Teren paid the one-copper market share to those who had worked all three
sets.

Me.

Marek.

Serra.

Iven had missed the third.

Orin had missed the first.

I held out my hand.

One copper.

Marek held out both.

"Why?"

"Intensity."

"One."

"Private market rate?"

"No."

"King rate?"

"No."

"Starvation?"

Rinna handed him a sausage.

Marek considered.

"Accepted."

Teren gave the remaining company copper to Rinna.

Not much.

The job had paid for part of the warehouse floor.

Or bread.

Or water.

Or something else.

It had also fed us.

That was apparently enough to make it worth staying until one.

Barely.

After lunch Teren disappeared with Dema.

I thought they were negotiating another performance.

They weren't.

Dema came back alone.

Teren went to the wagons.

"Pack."

Marek said, "Show?"

"No."

"Tonight?"

"No."

"Tomorrow?"

"Maybe."

"Money?"

"Maybe."

Marek looked at me.

"Strong industry."

Rinna asked, "Where?"

Teren held up another folded note.

"Mill."

"The answer?"

"Yes."

"Good?"

"Not no."

Davin said, "Road?"

Teren pointed southeast.

Davin frowned.

"Wheel."

Rinna said, "You said that yesterday."

"Still."

Teren looked at the sky.

Then at the square.

Then east.

"Dast?"

Rinna said, "Not yet."

He nodded.

"Mill. Slow."

That was the decision.

Half a day southeast if the road behaved.

Longer if Davin's face was accurate.

The mill settlement had not booked us.

Someone there had finally answered Teren.

That was enough to move.

I put my one market copper into my inner pocket.

It touched the scrap paper around Lyssa's clasp.

For a second I thought about buying something else in the market.

Then did not.

Not because I couldn't.

Nothing there needed buying.

That was new too.

Pell handed me the fish.

"Again?"

"Prop wagon."

"I know."

"Then why me?"

He had already walked away.

I carried it.

A woman with onions stepped directly into my path.

I moved.

She did not know I had been Sword beside her stall two hours earlier.

Maybe she did.

She did not care.

Good.

At the wagon, I put the fish with the props.

Our props.

I noticed it this time.

I left the word alone.

Davin checked the long box.

Dry.

Upright.

Unopened.

Rinna counted food.

Teren read the mill note again.

Serra stood near the bridge with her own folded note in one hand, not
reading it.

Orin had the cloth packet from yesterday inside his coat.

Marek had one copper and half a sausage.

Iven still had pig mud on one trouser leg.

The village market kept going without us.

We left at one forty.

Nobody applauded.

Nobody waved.

Dema was arguing with the potter before we reached the bridge.

The road southeast was bad.

Not dramatic.

Just slow.

Every rut took time.

Every bad edge made Davin choose.

The wagons moved carefully enough that walking people passed us twice.

I looked back once.

The village disappeared behind trees.

One copper in my pocket.

Lunch in my stomach.

No evening show.

Maybe work at the mill.

Dast somewhere beyond that.

Carrow somewhere behind us.

I had started thinking in one more stop.

That was not the same as deciding to stay.

It was also not the same as going home.

Marek woke when the wagon hit a hole.

"Money?"

"Maybe."

He nodded.

"Good."

Then he went back to sleep.

# CHAPTER 163

## THE MILL PLAYER

The road had opinions.

Mostly about wheels.

Every hundred yards it found a new way to express them.

The wagon dropped into another rut. Marek's head struck the sideboard.

He opened one eye.

"Money?"

"Still maybe."

"Wake me at yes."

He closed it.

Across from him, Serra had her folded note tucked under one thigh while
she mended a tear in her glove. She had not opened it since the bridge.

I looked away before she noticed me noticing.

The road climbed.

That was worse.

The ruts became shelves cut into hard dirt, some filled with yesterday's
water. Davin walked beside the lead wagon more often than he rode,
choosing where the wheels went one bad stretch at a time. When he lifted
one hand, the driver stopped. When he pointed, the wagon moved six
inches left or right.

Nobody argued.

I had seen Teren argue with hall owners, patrons, market masters,
actors, Rinna, weather, and once a chair.

He did not argue with Davin about roads.

That seemed sensible.

By late afternoon the land dropped again and we heard the mill before we
saw it.

Not a pleasant waterwheel turning beside flowers.

A mill.

The first sound was a deep wooden knocking under a constant rush of
water. Then came a grinding vibration I could feel through the wagon
boards. The road curved around a low hill and the settlement appeared
below us, spread along a narrow river that had been forced to behave.

A stone channel split away from the river upstream. Water ran fast
between retaining walls, crossed beneath a timber walkway, and struck a
broad wheel beside the largest building. The wheel was dark with spray.
Beyond it stood two long timber structures, a stone storehouse, sheds,
workers' cottages, a stable, and several grain barns with high doors.

Flour dust had gotten everywhere.

Roof edges.

Window ledges.

Cart wheels.

People.

A man came out of a doorway carrying a sack and looked as though someone
had thrown him into bread.

I noticed the sluice gate first.

Of course I noticed the sluice gate first.

I leaned.

Teren, riding ahead, turned around.

"No."

"I'm looking."

"That's how it starts."

"I don't even know what I'm looking at."

"Better."

We reached the bottom.

A wagon loaded with grain blocked the main yard.

Davin stopped us before the bridge.

"Wait."

The bridge was wide enough.

I could see that.

I almost said it.

Then a second grain wagon came out of the mill and took the entire
bridge while turning.

Fine.

We waited.

A woman walking beside it pointed at my crutch.

"Don't put that on the white boards."

I looked down.

Several boards along the edge of the yard were dusted pale.

"Why?"

"Chute."

"What chute?"

She pointed under them.

I looked.

There was a gap.

Not large.

Large enough for the bottom of a crutch to disappear into somewhere I
did not want to follow.

"Good."

"Not really."

She kept walking.

Local competence.

Annoying.

Useful.

When the bridge cleared, Davin took the wagons across one at a time.

The long box moved with them.

Upright.

Dry.

Unopened.

Nobody in the mill yard looked twice.

They had grain to move.

A boy came running from the office building.

"Players?"

Teren said, "Yes."

The boy pointed.

"Vessa's in the count room."

"Which?"

He pointed at the stone building.

"Count room."

Teren started walking.

Rinna followed.

Marek sat up.

"Money?"

Teren did not turn.

"Not yet."

Marek lay back down.

I got off the wagon because my back wanted something different.

Pell handed me a bundle of costume cloth.

"Why?"

"Keep it off the flour."

"Where?"

He pointed at the flour.

"Not there."

Then he ran toward Nessa.

Good.

I stood in an industrial yard holding fabric.

A cart came toward me.

I moved.

Another cart came from the other direction.

I moved again.

The woman who had warned me about the chute passed back through.

"You're in the loading lane."

"Where isn't?"

She pointed toward a strip beside the stone wall.

I went there.

The cloth remained off the flour.

Success.

A bell rang.

I nearly dropped it.

Doors opened all across the mill.

Workers came out.

Not everyone.

Enough to suddenly make the yard belong to a shift instead of wagons.

Some headed toward the cottages. Some went to a pump. Three men sat
directly on grain sacks and started eating. A woman washed her face in a
bucket and made the water white.

Iven came over.

"Show?"

"I don't know."

"Why are you holding that?"

"I don't know."

He nodded.

"Good."

The count room door opened.

Teren came out.

Rinna did not.

Behind him was a broad woman with cropped brown hair and a flour streak
across one cheek. She wore a dark vest over rolled sleeves and had two
pencils tucked through the same buttonhole.

"Vessa," Teren said.

She looked at us.

Not me.

All of us.

"Which one's the manager?"

Marek pointed at himself.

Teren said, "Me."

Vessa looked at Marek.

"Why did he point?"

"Illness."

"Permanent?"

"Probably."

Marek said, "I can hear you."

Vessa nodded.

"Good."

She was the one who had answered.

Not no meant exactly what it sounded like.

She could offer us a place.

She could offer food.

She could offer some money.

She could not offer enough money.

"Owner won't pay for a troupe," she said.

Teren said, "Then why did you write?"

"Owner isn't the only person here."

"Who is paying?"

"Me. Partly."

"Personally?"

"Mill account."

"Owner knows?"

"Owner knows the account exists."

Teren stared at her.

Vessa stared back.

I liked her.

Rinna came out carrying a scrap of paper.

"How much?"

Vessa named the number again.

This time I heard it.

Twenty copper guaranteed.

For the company.

Not each.

Twenty.

More than the market.

Less than a full public show if everyone had to be paid normal rates.

Teren said, "No."

Vessa said, "I know."

That was apparently why it had been not no.

She continued.

"Workers asked."

"All of them?"

"No."

"How many?"

"Enough to be annoying."

A man carrying a sack shouted from across the yard, "We heard that."

Vessa shouted back, "Work."

He kept walking.

Teren asked, "Door?"

"No door."

"Collection?"

"Maybe."

"Maybe isn't money."

"Neither is an empty evening."

Rinna looked at the paper.

"Lodging?"

"Store loft."

"Dry?"

"Yes."

"How many?"

"All."

"Food?"

"Tonight."

"Breakfast?"

"No."

"Water?"

Vessa pointed at the pump.

"Free until the owner discovers thirst."

Rinna ignored that.

"Animals?"

"Stable space. Oats not included."

Davin, who had appeared behind us without sound, said, "How much?"

Vessa named a number.

He looked at Rinna.

Rinna frowned.

Teren said, "What do they want?"

Vessa shrugged.

"Something after second shift."

"Full play?"

"They don't know what that means."

Marek looked offended.

"Everyone knows what a play is."

A worker passing with a handcart said, "Is it singing?"

Marek said, "No."

The worker said, "Good."

Marek looked more offended.

Vessa pointed toward a long shed beyond the storehouse.

"Meal room. Benches. One end clear if we move tables."

"How many?"

"Workers?"

"Seats."

"Sixty if they like each other."

"And if they don't?"

"Forty."

Teren looked at Rinna.

Rinna looked at Davin.

Davin said, "Road bad."

"Thank you," Teren said.

"Tomorrow worse if rain."

We all looked up.

Clouds.

Not dramatic ones.

Just enough.

Vessa said, "You stay, you're under roof."

Rinna asked, "Twenty copper, dinner, loft, stable space."

"Yes."

"Plus collection."

Vessa said, "I won't force them."

Teren said, "Neither will we."

"Then yes."

"Collection belongs to company."

Vessa shrugged.

"Workers' money belongs to workers until they give it to you."

"Good."

"How long?"

"Forty minutes."

Vessa laughed.

"Twenty-five."

"Thirty-five."

"Twenty-five."

"Thirty."

"Done."

Teren held out his hand.

Vessa shook it.

That was the job.

Thirty minutes after second shift.

Twenty copper guaranteed.

Dinner.

Dry floor.

Whatever the workers voluntarily put into a collection afterward.

No normal show rate.

Again.

Marek said, "What do we get?"

Teren turned.

"Food."

"I am beginning to suspect this industry is mostly food."

Rinna said, "You're still here."

"Evidence."

Iven looked at me.

I looked at him.

We both said, "No."

Jurisdiction stayed dead.

Teren decided individual pay would depend on the collection.

That made Marek unhappy.

"Guaranteed?"

"No."

"We have guaranteed company money."

"Company has guaranteed company money."

"I remain company."

Rinna said, "You remain expensive."

"Privately."

"Always."

Teren clapped once.

"Unload what we need. Nothing else."

The meal room was exactly what Vessa had promised.

A long room with plank walls, low beams, six heavy tables, benches, two
small windows, and flour dust in places flour dust should not have been.

No stage.

No wings.

No curtain.

One door at each end.

The room smelled like bread before bread became food.

I immediately looked at the beams.

No.

Not a puzzle.

Just beams.

Pell sneezed four times.

Nessa said, "Costumes stay covered."

Pell sneezed again.

"Yes."

Teren walked the room.

"Mixed bill."

Marek said, "King."

"Short."

"King."

"Short King."

Marek considered.

"Insulting."

"Survive."

Teren pointed.

"Sword. Shopkeeper. Death."

Orin, standing in the doorway, said, "No."

Teren said, "Quiet."

"Not here."

"Why?"

Orin looked at the tables.

"Wrong room."

That was all.

Teren accepted it.

No death piece.

Instead Iven suggested the creditor scene, a short King argument, Sword,
and something Serra called the widow piece.

I did not know the widow piece.

"Am I in it?"

"No."

"Good."

"You're moving benches."

Less good.

Vessa gave me and Iven four workers to help rearrange the room.

I made the mistake of assuming they wanted me to tell them where the
benches went.

They did not.

A narrow man named Joss had apparently arranged this room for every
feast, fight, meeting, wage dispute, funeral meal, and winter card night
for eleven years.

I pointed at a bench.

"Maybe there?"

Joss said, "No."

"Why?"

"Door."

I looked.

It was not blocking the door.

Then the door opened and six workers came through carrying bowls.

Fine.

"Where?"

He pointed.

We put it there.

I stopped suggesting.

That improved me enormously.

The mounting board for Sword went against the far wall.

I tested the route.

Dry floor.

Mostly.

Near the kitchen end someone had spilled something greasy.

Joss saw me looking.

"Don't."

"Yes."

He threw sawdust over it.

Flour mill.

Sawdust.

I did not ask.

I had enough problems.

At some point I realized I had left one crutch against a bench while
helping shift the other end of it.

Then Joss moved the bench.

My crutch went with it.

I spent two minutes looking for it while everyone else worked.

Not charming.

Just stupid.

Serra found it.

She held it out.

"Missing something?"

"No."

She looked at my leg.

"Fair."

I took it.

"Thank you."

"Don't do that onstage."

"I'll try."

She walked away.

Her folded note was no longer visible.

None of my business.

The mill ran around us until the second bell.

That was the strangest part.

We were preparing entertainment inside somebody else's workday.

Every few minutes the floor trembled faintly.

Water hammered outside.

Sacks moved.

Doors opened.

People shouted weights.

A cart wheel squealed for ten straight minutes until Davin disappeared
toward it and came back with grease on one hand.

"Did you fix their cart?"

"No."

"Then why?"

He looked at his hand.

"Wheel."

I stopped.

Dinner came before the performance.

Vessa had promised food and meant worker food.

Thick stew.

Dark bread.

Boiled roots.

Onions.

Marek looked at the bowl.

"Again?"

Rinna said, "Eat."

"I like onions."

"Then why complain?"

"I contain multitudes."

Orin said, "No."

We ate with the first shift while the second shift finished.

Some workers knew we were performers.

Some did not.

A woman across from me asked whether we sold tools.

"No."

She pointed at the Sword mounting board.

"What's that?"

"Me."

She looked at it.

Then at me.

"Bad tool."

"Apparently."

She went back to eating.

Tiny fame.

Good.

A younger man had heard of the company name from somewhere west.

Not me.

He remembered Marek.

"The shouting one?"

Marek sat straighter.

"King."

"Right."

Marek looked pleased.

The man added, "My cousin said you died."

Marek's face changed.

"Different play."

"Probably."

Serra laughed into her stew.

At the far table two workers were arguing about whether management
should have paid twenty copper for actors when one of the grain lifts
needed a new rope.

Vessa heard them.

"So fix the rope."

"We told you."

"Then tell Brann."

"We told Brann."

"Then tell him louder."

One of them pointed at Marek.

"Can we borrow him?"

Vessa looked at Marek.

"Maybe after."

That was the mill audience.

Not grateful workers waiting for culture.

People who had been working all day and had opinions about rope.

The second bell rang while I was still eating.

Everyone at three tables stood almost at once.

I thought it meant we were starting.

I put down my spoon.

Iven said, "What are you doing?"

"Bell."

"Shift."

"Oh."

They left.

Five minutes later a different group came in.

I sat back down.

Marek saw.

"Veteran."

"Fuck you."

"Passenger."

I threw bread at him.

Rinna caught it before it landed.

"Food."

"Sorry."

She ate it.

The performance began after dark.

Not immediately after shift.

Workers washed.

Changed shirts.

Found beer.

Some went home.

Some came back with spouses or older children.

Nobody charged admission.

A wooden bowl sat near the door.

No sign.

No announcement.

Collection.

The room filled to maybe fifty.

Then emptied to forty-five when someone shouted about a horse.

Then returned to fifty-two.

I stopped counting.

Teren did not ask me to.

The King piece went first.

Short.

Marek stood on a table until Vessa said, "No."

He got down.

"Authority."

She pointed at the ceiling.

"Beam."

Fair.

The piece worked.

Not beautifully.

A man in the back talked through half of it about oats.

Serra waited once until he realized everyone could hear him.

He stopped.

She continued.

No speech.

Shopkeeper came second.

Iven owed me money.

Simple.

Portable.

The first line got nothing.

The second got less.

A woman near the door yawned.

I could hear cups.

At the market I had learned that people could leave.

Here they could stay and still not care.

Different problem.

Iven tried to make the debt larger.

I said, "You don't have larger."

He said, "I work at a mill."

A worker shouted, "Then he's broke!"

That got them.

I looked at Iven.

"Employment is not evidence."

He stared at me.

I had done it.

Not jurisdiction.

Worse.

The room laughed.

Iven said, "You promised."

"I promised nothing."

"Good."

"Pay me."

We moved.

The scene got better after that because the workers started offering
reasons Iven should not pay.

Children.

Rent.

Beer.

Bad flour.

One man shouted, "Rope!"

Vessa shouted from the back, "Tomorrow!"

I said, "Add it to his debt."

That was dangerous.

It worked.

I did not repeat it.

Sword came later.

Pell had not brought the fish.

Good.

The room was close enough that I could see flour in people's hair.

Serra took Sword from the wall.

A worker said, "That's the tool."

The woman from dinner said, "Bad tool."

I said, "Repeat customer."

She laughed.

Then someone near the door left.

Fine.

The scene continued.

Marek forgot a line.

Serra supplied the question he needed.

I answered too early once.

She looked at me.

I waited.

She gave the actual line.

I answered again.

Nobody died.

Work.

Halfway through, the mill wheel changed sound.

Not stopped.

Changed.

Three workers looked toward the wall.

So did Vessa.

Nobody moved.

The sound settled.

The workers looked back.

I had no idea what had happened.

Serra had continued speaking.

I had missed my cue.

"Well?" she said.

I looked at her.

Then at the wall.

"Your castle is making noises."

A worker shouted, "Not ours!"

I said, "Excellent. Then we can leave."

That got enough laughter to cover the gap.

Serra continued.

Later I asked Joss what the sound had been.

He said, "Gate."

"What happened?"

"Changed water."

"Why?"

"Needed less."

That was all.

Not a mystery.

Not my mill.

The widow piece closed.

I watched from the side.

Serra and Orin were in it after all, but it was not the death piece.
Orin played a man trying to sell a widow her own chair because he
claimed her dead husband had owed him for it.

I looked at Iven.

He whispered, "Don't."

"I didn't say anything."

"You leaned."

Fuck.

The workers liked it more than Sword.

Good.

At the end there was applause.

Real enough.

Not huge.

A few people left before it finished.

One child was asleep across two chairs.

Teren stepped forward.

"Thank you."

That was it.

No extra piece.

No request.

No emergency.

The bowl by the door filled slowly as people left.

Copper.

Mostly.

One button.

Someone had put in a nail.

Marek picked up the nail.

"Money?"

Rinna said, "No."

"Investment?"

"No."

Orin looked at him.

Marek put it back.

When the room emptied, Vessa counted twenty copper into Teren's hand.

Guaranteed.

Teren gave it directly to Rinna.

Then Rinna counted the bowl.

Seventeen copper.

A button.

The nail.

And one tiny silver shaving so thin I was not sure it had ever been a
coin.

Rinna looked at Vessa.

Vessa shrugged.

"Workers."

Teren said, "Thirty-seven copper."

Rinna said, "Plus food. Plus floor."

"Minus oats."

"Davin?"

Davin named the stable cost.

Rinna's mouth tightened.

Not disaster.

Not triumph.

Work.

Teren paid individual shares from the collection.

Two copper each for the performers who had done the full mixed bill.

I got two.

Marek got two.

Serra got two.

Iven got two.

Orin got two.

Others got different amounts depending on what they had done.

I did not count theirs.

Marek held his two copper like a man restored to society.

"Mill money."

I said, "Don't invest it."

He looked offended.

"You don't support enterprise."

"What was the investment?"

Orin said, "No."

Marek pointed.

"Confidential."

Still no answer.

We slept in the store loft above sacks of grain.

Dry.

Free with the job.

No beds.

Better than paying for a warehouse floor.

Before sleep, Teren and Rinna talked quietly near the ladder.

Not secret.

Just work.

"Enough?" Teren asked.

"For tomorrow."

"Dast?"

"Still weak."

"Mill north road?"

Davin, from somewhere in the dark, said, "Better."

Teren said, "I wasn't asking you."

"Yes."

Rinna laughed once.

Then said, "There is a town east of here. Brann says market day the day
after tomorrow."

"Hall?"

"Assembly room."

"Answer?"

"None."

Teren was quiet.

Then: "We try."

"Dast?"

"After."

Not confirmed.

Nothing was confirmed.

That seemed to be the road.

I lay down.

My two mill copper went into my pocket with the market copper, the rest
of my wages, and Lyssa's wrapped brass clasp.

One more stop.

The phrase had become easier.

That probably meant I should distrust it.

I didn't.

Below us, the mill wheel kept turning in the dark.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 164

## THE PROSPECTOR

The mill started before I did.

I woke to grain moving under my head.

Not metaphorically.

A sack hit the floor below the loft hard enough to shake dust out of the
boards. Someone shouted a number. Someone else shouted a different
number. The wheel was already turning, the grinding vibration had
returned, and pale flour floated through a blade of morning light beside
the loft door.

Pell slept through all of it.

Iven did not.

He was sitting against a sack with his boots on, eating an apple.

"Breakfast?"

"Mine."

"Helpful."

"You asked what it was."

Below us, a man shouted, "Need the loft!"

That woke Pell.

He sat up.

"Fire?"

"No."

"Fish?"

"No."

He went back down.

I kicked his boot.

"Loft."

"Oh."

The company came apart from sleep quickly.

Blankets rolled.

Bags closed.

Costumes disappeared into covers before flour could settle on them.
Nessa found a white handprint on one bundle and stared at Pell until he
denied touching anything.

"I was asleep."

"You have hands while asleep."

"Unfair."

Rinna climbed the ladder carrying the wooden collection bowl from last
night.

The nail was still in it.

Marek had apparently not invested it.

"Out," she said.

Nobody asked why.

The mill needed the loft.

We left.

Vessa passed us in the yard with a ledger under one arm and a man
talking at her about the grain-lift rope.

He said, "I told Brann."

"Tell him again."

"He knows."

"Then make knowing expensive."

She saw Teren.

"Road east is clear."

Davin said, "Mostly."

Vessa looked at him.

"You've been?"

"Asked."

"Who?"

"Cart."

She accepted that.

Teren said, "Thank you."

Vessa nodded once.

Then the rope man said something else and we stopped existing.

Good.

Joss was moving tables back into the meal room.

I passed the door.

He pointed at one bench.

"Wrong."

"I didn't touch it."

"I know."

That somehow felt worse.

Breakfast had not been included.

Rinna made this everybody's problem in an organized way.

We still had bread from the road food, several apples, hard cheese, and
the last of something that might once have been roast meat. Marek
reached for the meat.

Rinna slapped his hand.

"That's noon."

"What is morning?"

"Bread."

"Morning deserves dignity."

"Buy dignity."

Marek checked his purse.

Morning lost.

A woman near the mill gate sold hot oat cakes from a covered basket. One
copper bought two.

I had money.

That fact was still strange enough that I stood there for a moment deciding whether hot food was worth one copper.

Then I bought it.

No debate.

No calculation about whether I could survive without it.

One cake went into my mouth.

The other went into my pocket for later.

That felt more significant than it deserved.

Marek watched.

"You have wealth."

"I have breakfast."

"Same thing."

"You have two copper."

"Reserved."

"For what?"

"Opportunity."

Orin walked past us.

"No."

Marek pointed after him.

"He fears enterprise."

We left the mill before eight.

Nobody waved.

The wheel kept turning.

A grain wagon was already waiting for the bridge before our last wagon
crossed it.

The road east really was better.

Not good.

Better.

For almost half an hour we managed a speed that made the wagons feel
like transportation instead of furniture. Then a flock of sheep occupied
the road and reduced us to walking behind them while one boy and an
elderly dog argued about direction. Davin did not complain. Teren did
not complain. Marek complained enough for everyone.

The sheep ignored him.

Eventually the boy got them into a field and lifted one hand in apology.

Davin lifted his back.

That seemed to settle the matter.

There were fewer ruts deep enough to have names, and stretches had been
laid with crushed stone. We made enough speed that Marek stayed awake.

This proved unfortunate.

He spent the first hour attempting to determine what kind of town we
were approaching.

"Rich?"

Teren said, "No."

"Poor?"

"No."

"Violent?"

"Probably."

"Useful?"

"Unknown."

"Women?"

Serra said, "Almost certainly."

"Excellent."

She threw an apple core at him.

He caught it.

"Breakfast."

The land opened as we traveled. Grain fields gave way to pasture and
fenced lots. We passed cattle moving west, then sheep, then three wagons
loaded with empty cages that smelled as if the cages had recently
contained something deeply committed to being alive.

By midday we began passing people headed the same direction.

Carts.

Farmers.

A family walking beside two goats.

A man leading a bull with the expression of someone who had made several
poor choices and was committed to all of them.

Market day tomorrow.

The road knew before the town did.

Rinna sat beside Teren with a folded scrap on her knee.

"No answer," she said.

"I know."

"Could have changed."

"Could have."

"Could be full."

"Could be."

"Could be nothing."

Teren looked at her.

"We try."

Rinna folded the paper.

That was apparently the entire strategy.

At a crossroads we stopped for water.

There was a stone trough, a shrine, a blacksmith's shed, and a woman
selling boiled eggs under a cloth.

Marek spent one copper.

Reserved opportunity became egg.

He ate it in three bites.

"Investment?"

"Protein."

"Profitable?"

"Immediately."

Davin checked the wheels.

Rinna checked the horses.

Pell discovered a burr attached to his trousers and accused the
countryside.

Nessa removed it.

Serra sat on the low shrine wall writing something.

Not reading.

Writing.

I saw the folded paper beside her.

I looked toward the road.

None of my business.

I took out the oat cake I had saved.

It had flattened into a warm disk with pocket lint on one edge.

I ate the other edge.

I thought about Lyssa.

Not because of anything important.

Because she would have told me not to eat pocket lint and then watched
to see whether I did.

I touched the inner pocket where the brass clasp sat wrapped in scrap
paper.

Still there.

My letter might be in Carrow by now.

Or in a wagon.

Or under somebody's soup.

I had no idea.

For the first time it occurred to me that Lyssa could answer and have
nowhere sensible to send the answer.

I asked Teren.

"How do letters find you?"

He looked at me.

"They usually don't."

"Helpful."

"If I know a route, I leave names at halls and inns."

"And if you don't know the route?"

"They don't."

"So people just miss letters?"

"Yes."

"That seems badly designed."

"The road?"

"Mail."

"The road too."

He drank water.

"If you're writing again, send to Carrow and tell them to hold replies
at East Market Hall."

"Will we be there?"

"Eventually."

"When?"

He looked at the wagons.

"No."

Fair.

I did not write another letter.

Not yet.

We reached the town in the middle of the afternoon.

It announced itself with fences.

Long ones.

Heavy ones.

Pens spread along the western edge in a rough grid, some empty, some
holding sheep, pigs, goats, or cattle. The smell arrived before the
buildings did. Beyond the pens stood a broad market square, two inns, a
row of shops, a smithy, a low brick counting house, and a whitewashed
building with tall double doors.

The assembly room.

Probably.

A painted sign beside the road said KEST.

Below that, someone had nailed a smaller board:

MARKET TOMORROW.

Below that, someone had written:

NO PIGS IN EAST YARD.

A pig stood in the east yard.

Good town.

We pulled into a wagon field behind the first inn.

A man came out before the wheels stopped.

"Stabling?"

Teren said, "Maybe."

"Maybe costs one copper."

"Looking costs?"

"Free."

Teren looked.

The man looked back.

Rinna climbed down.

"Water?"

"Included if stabled."

"Oats?"

"Separate."

"Loft?"

"Full."

"Rooms?"

"Nearly."

"Market."

"Exactly."

Rinna's face did a small thing.

Money.

We had arrived on the expensive side of tomorrow.

Teren said, "Assembly room."

The innkeeper pointed across the square.

"Ask Noll."

"Where?"

"Depends."

"On what?"

"Whether he owes you money."

Marek said, "I like him."

Teren ignored Marek.

"Who is Noll?"

"Keeper."

"Where?"

"Try cattle office."

Teren started across the square.

Then stopped.

He pointed at me.

"Come."

I looked behind me.

Nobody else.

"Why?"

"Door."

"What door?"

"Assembly room."

"I can see it."

"Good. Check it."

Apparently I had been promoted to door.

We crossed the square.

Market preparation was already swallowing the town.

People marked spaces with chalk.

A woman hammered stakes beside a cloth awning.

Two boys rolled barrels toward an inn.

Cattle complained from the western pens.

A man carrying six wooden stools nearly walked into me, then blamed me
with his face.

I moved.

The assembly room sat beside the counting house.

The front doors were broad.

Too broad to be interesting.

Teren tried one.

Locked.

He knocked.

Nothing.

A woman arranging baskets across the street shouted, "Noll!"

Teren shouted back, "Where?"

She pointed vaguely east.

"Office!"

"Which office?"

"Cattle!"

Good.

We went to the cattle office.

Noll was not there.

A clerk with ink on both hands said, "Market office."

We went to the market office.

Noll was not there.

A boy said, "Pens."

"Which pens?"

The boy looked offended.

"Cattle."

Back to cattle.

Teren stopped in the middle of the square.

"Do you know what he looks like?"

"No."

"Good."

"How are we finding him?"

"Eventually he'll become annoyed enough to find us."

That sounded like experience.

He handed me a folded note.

"If you see Noll, give him this."

"How will I know?"

"Ask."

Then Teren left me.

I had not understood the assignment.

I thought I was checking a door.

Now I was hunting a man nobody could locate.

Touring.

I asked the basket woman.

"Noll?"

"Red vest."

"Thank you."

"Unless he changed."

"Today?"

"Since noon."

Fine.

I asked a cattle drover.

"Noll?"

"Short."

I asked a woman carrying a chicken upside down.

"Noll?"

"Annoying."

We were narrowing him down.

At the east pens I found a short man in a red vest arguing with three
people at once.

One wanted another livestock space.

One wanted money back.

One wanted pigs moved.

The pig problem had spread.

I waited.

He noticed me.

"What?"

"Noll?"

"No."

I looked at the red vest.

He looked at it too.

"Brother."

"Where's Noll?"

"Assembly room."

Of course.

I went back.

The doors were open.

Teren stood inside with a tall bald man holding a ring of keys.

Noll.

He was not short.

He wore no red.

I handed him the note.

He opened it.

"This was for me?"

"Apparently."

"You've been carrying it?"

"For twelve minutes."

Teren said, "Excellent."

I looked at him.

"You knew?"

"No."

"Worse."

Noll read.

"No."

There it was.

Clean.

Teren said, "Room?"

"No."

"Tomorrow?"

"Committee has it."

"For?"

"Market supper."

"Night?"

"Market supper."

"After?"

"Cleaning."

"Before?"

"Setup."

Teren looked around.

The assembly room was better than the mill meal room and worse than an
actual theatre.

High ceiling.

Small platform at one end.

Windows along both walls.

A side door.

A kitchen hatch.

Stacked benches.

No backstage.

No curtain.

No reason for us to be there.

Teren said, "Tonight."

Noll looked at him.

"Tonight what?"

"Room."

"No."

"Why?"

"Empty."

"That's why."

Noll frowned.

"Nobody's coming tonight."

"Could."

"Who?"

"People."

Noll stared.

Teren waited.

I leaned against the wall.

This was not acting.

Probably.

Noll said, "Room costs eight copper."

"Four."

"Eight."

"No audience."

"Your problem."

"No heat."

"Six."

"Eight."

"Benches included?"

"Obviously."

"Kitchen?"

"No."

"Side room?"

"No."

"Seven."

Noll said, "Eight."

Teren said, "No."

Then he walked out.

I followed.

That was apparently negotiation.

Outside, I asked, "Are we done?"

"No."

"You said no."

"He said eight."

"You said no."

"Yes."

"That sounds done."

"It isn't."

I hated this job.

Rinna found us near the wagon field.

"Room?"

"Eight."

"No."

"Yes."

"Lodging?"

"Bad."

"How bad?"

She told him.

Teren swore.

Not loudly.

The private-house silver was no longer abstract.

Neither was the mill money.

Rooms, oats, stabling, food, room rental.

A town could eat a job before the job existed.

Rinna said, "We can camp outside."

"Weather?"

Davin looked up.

"Dry."

"For once."

"Maybe."

Teren rubbed his face.

"Market committee?"

"Tonight," Rinna said. "Counting house. Six."

"Who told you?"

"Man with pigs."

"Reliable?"

"He had three."

That was enough.

We waited.

That was the work.

Not rehearsing.

Not performing.

Waiting for six.

The company spread through Kest because there was nothing else to do.

Nessa and Pell found a cloth seller.

Davin went somewhere involving horses.

Orin disappeared.

Marek discovered a dice game behind the second inn and, to my surprise,
did not join it.

He stood watching.

"Growth?" I asked.

"Capital preservation."

"You have one copper."

"Exactly."

Serra bought a cup of something hot and sat on a fence watching cattle.

I sat beside her.

Not too close.

The fence was wide.

"You know anyone here?" I asked.

"No."

That was it.

Good.

A cow sneezed on Marek when he walked past.

Better.

At six the market committee met.

Teren went in.

Rinna went with him.

We did not.

I bought a bowl of beans for one copper because dinner was not included
anywhere and nobody had promised it would be.

The bowl was hot.

I could afford it.

I ate beside the wagons while Pell tried to teach the wooden fish to
bite on command.

"Doesn't it already?"

"Sometimes."

"That's not teaching."

"It knows independence."

The fish snapped.

Pell smiled.

I moved my hand.

At dusk Teren came back.

Marek stood.

"Money?"

"Maybe."

Marek looked at me.

I said, "Don't."

Teren held up a paper.

The committee would not pay a guarantee.

They would let us use part of the south market edge tomorrow after
livestock judging.

No charge.

We could collect.

No room.

No company fee.

No food.

No lodging.

Rinna said, "That's not work."

Teren said, "Could be."

"Could be twelve copper."

"Could be forty."

"Could be six."

"Yes."

"Dast?"

He looked east.

"Still after."

Rinna folded her arms.

The assembly room doors across the square opened.

Men began carrying tables inside for tomorrow's supper.

Eight copper.

No audience.

The market square would cost nothing.

Maybe audience.

Maybe money.

Maybe not.

Teren looked at us.

"Tomorrow. One set first."

Marek said, "One?"

"If they stop, two."

"If they pay?"

"If they pay."

"And if they don't?"

"We leave."

Simple.

Rinna sighed.

"Where do we sleep?"

Teren pointed west.

Beyond the livestock pens, outside the town wall, was a flat field
already filling with market wagons and temporary camps.

Free.

Probably.

Marek looked at it.

"Private money was better."

I said, "Private beds were better."

"We had a loft."

"Private floor was better."

"Fair."

We moved the wagons before dark.

Davin chose a place away from the lowest ground.

Rinna paid for oats.

Nothing else.

No room.

No warehouse.

No stable loft.

We ate what remained of the road food and what people bought for
themselves.

The town kept building tomorrow around us.

Lanterns appeared.

Animals settled badly.

People shouted across camps.

Somebody sang near a wagon until somebody else told them to stop.

I lay under the wagon with my blanket and looked at the dark shape of
the assembly-room roof beyond the pens.

We had come east for work.

We had found no guarantee.

We were staying anyway.

One set.

Then maybe another.

Then maybe Dast.

Maybe.

I put a hand over the pocket with Lyssa's clasp.

One more stop had become one more morning.

That was probably how it happened.

# CHAPTER 165

## THE PLAYER

A cow woke me by objecting to commerce.

It began before sunrise and continued until I accepted that whatever
argument the cow was making had already been lost. By then three other
cattle had joined it, somebody was hammering stakes into the ground, two
wagon wheels were grinding over stone nearby, and a man somewhere beyond
our camp was shouting that six was not eight.

Another man shouted back that the animal had four legs.

This did not settle the matter.

I opened my eyes under the wagon.

Market day.

The flat field beyond Kest had changed while we slept. Cooking smoke
hung low between wagons. Traders folded blankets, tightened harness,
checked ropes, cursed animals, counted baskets, and shouted names I did
not know. A boy ran past carrying a chicken. The chicken appeared to
disagree with the route.

Pell was asleep beside one wagon wheel with the wooden fish tucked under
his arm.

Iven stepped over him.

"Dead?"

"Probably."

"The fish?"

"No."

Pell opened one eye.

"Rude."

Breakfast cost money.

Rinna solved part of this by buying a pot of oat porridge from a camp
cook for the company, which meant everybody got something warm and
nobody got enough to mistake it for generosity. She paid from company
copper. Marek watched the transaction closely.

"How much?"

"Not yours."

"I am learning."

"Learn farther away."

I bought nothing else.

My bowl was enough.

Marek ate his, then stood beside the pot until Rinna noticed.

Rinna covered the pot.

"Breakfast is finished."

"I haven't asked."

"Then we're done."

Davin had already moved the wagons closer to the south side of town
before most of us finished eating. The long iron-cornered box rode where
it always rode, upright, tied, dry, uninteresting to everybody except
the people who had to move around it.

Pell reached toward one of Davin's ropes.

Davin said, "No."

Pell withdrew his hand.

"Good," I said.

Davin looked at me.

I stopped helping.

By full morning, Kest had become louder than the mill.

The livestock pens filled first.

Cattle in the western runs.

Sheep farther south.

Pigs near the east yard despite the sign.

Goats wherever goats had decided they belonged.

The broad market square filled with cloth awnings and temporary tables.
People sold harness, knives, pots, onions, boots, cheese, salt, cheap
ribbons, baskets, wooden tools, live birds, dead birds, and things in
jars I could not identify from a safe distance.

The company had been given part of the south market edge.

That sounded larger when Teren said it yesterday.

In practice, it was a strip of packed earth between a sheep pen, a cart
lane, and a woman selling onions.

The onion woman looked at our wagon.

"No."

Teren said, "We have permission."

"Not there."

"Committee said south edge."

"That's south lane."

She pointed with an onion.

"Cart comes through there."

Teren looked at the lane.

It looked exactly like empty ground.

A cart came through it.

Teren moved.

The woman nodded.

Local expertise.

A market official arrived wearing a green sash and carrying a stick with
chalk marks on it. He was called Harven. That was all I learned about
him because he was already late for something else.

He pointed.

"From that post to the trough."

Teren said, "That's narrow."

"Yes."

"Collection?"

"Fine."

"Bench?"

"No."

"Mounting board?"

Harven looked at the Sword board.

"What is it?"

"Performance."

"No nails."

"We don't nail it."

"Good."

"How long?"

"Judging clears by eleven. You have until the wool auction."

"When?"

"Depends on sheep."

Then he left.

Marek watched him go.

"I respect that."

"You don't understand any of it," Serra said.

"Exactly."

We waited for sheep.

That was most of the morning.

There were too many people to perform and nowhere to perform because the
south edge belonged to livestock judging until livestock judging stopped
belonging to it. Teren walked the boundary twice. Rinna talked to the
onion woman. Nessa kept costumes inside the wagon because the ground was
already filthy. Orin vanished and returned with a paper cone of roasted
seeds.

Nobody asked where he had been.

Serra stood at the sheep pen watching a judge put his hands on an animal
with deep professional seriousness.

"Can he tell?"

I asked.

"Tell what?"

"Which sheep."

She looked at me.

"Yes."

"Helpful."

"You asked."

A goat began chewing the corner of a cloth sign.

Its owner removed the sign from the goat.

The goat looked offended.

At ten thirty, Teren told me to watch the collection bowl.

"We aren't collecting."

"Watch it anyway."

The wooden bowl sat on the wagon step.

"What am I watching for?"

"Children."

That made sense five minutes later.

A girl picked it up.

I said, "That's ours."

She looked inside.

"It's empty."

"Still ours."

"Why?"

"Future money."

She considered this.

"Bad bowl."

Then she put it down.

I had successfully defended company assets from a seven-year-old critic.

At eleven, the sheep moved.

Not all at once.

Nothing at Kest happened all at once.

One pen emptied. Another filled. Men dragged temporary barriers away.
