Harven reappeared, pointed at our strip, and said, "Now."

Teren said, "How long?"

Harven was already walking.

"Sheep."

Useful.

The company moved.

Fast.

Davin and Pell carried the mounting board.

Nessa brought only what costumes were needed.

Rinna put the collection bowl near the front edge and then moved it
because the onion woman said a cart wheel would crush it.

I carried a bundle of cloth to the wrong side.

Nessa said, "Other."

I moved it.

"Other."

"There are only two."

"Behind."

There were three.

Fine.

Teren chose the first set while we were setting it.

"King opening. Short. Sword. Orin closes."

"No Shopkeeper?" I asked.

"Not first."

Marek smiled.

"Headliner."

"No," Teren said.

"King."

"Noise."

Marek's smile weakened.

"Royal noise."

"Get dressed."

We had no curtain.

No backstage.

No raised platform.

The crowd did not know a performance was beginning because the crowd did
not care.

Marek solved this by climbing onto the low mounting block and shouting:

"Citizens!"

Three people looked.

Teren closed his eyes.

Marek continued.

"I have been robbed!"

More people looked.

A cattle buyer shouted, "Again?"

Marek pointed at him.

"Of respect!"

The cattle buyer laughed.

That helped.

Serra entered from beside the onion stall wearing the Princess coat.
Iven came in from the wagon lane. Orin appeared from somewhere behind a
cheese seller.

The scene began.

Not the play.

A piece of it.

Compressed.

Loud enough to compete with sheep.

I stood beside the mounting board waiting for Sword.

At first maybe fifteen people stopped.

Then twenty.

Then fewer because a line of cattle moved past and took half the view
with them.

Marek raised his voice.

A horse near the trough raised its head.

Teren made a small downward motion.

Marek ignored him for one line.

Then heard himself.

He lowered it.

The horse went back to being a horse.

By the time Serra came for the Sword, we had a real half-circle.

Not a hall audience.

Nobody sat.

People held baskets.

One man kept negotiating the price of a bridle while watching over the
seller's shoulder.

A woman bounced a baby.

Two boys had climbed the sheep fence.

The onion woman watched while still selling onions.

Serra stopped in front of me.

"I require a weapon."

I said, "You require judgment."

A man walking past laughed without stopping.

No copper.

Serra said, "I have judgment."

"Then why are you here?"

That got more.

Someone dropped a copper into the bowl.

I heard it.

That was different.

Applause could happen at the end.

Money made a sound immediately.

Serra took the Sword.

The woman who had bought onions said, "Is that the sword?"

The onion seller said, "Apparently."

I almost looked at her.

Did not.

Serra continued.

I answered.

The crowd grew.

Then a goat put its head through the fence behind me and bit the bottom
corner of the mounting cloth.

I felt the pull.

I looked down.

Wrong.

Serra was giving me a line.

I missed it.

She waited half a beat.

"Do you object?"

The goat pulled again.

"To theft," I said.

The crowd saw the goat.

That helped too much.

A boy shouted, "He's eating him!"

I said, "Slowly."

Laugh.

Copper.

Another copper.

The goat's owner arrived and dragged it backward.

The cloth came free with a wet corner.

Nessa made a sound from behind the wagon that I would hear later in my
sleep.

I should have checked the cloth before we started.

I had put the mounting board too close to the pen.

Nobody else had.

Me.

The scene continued.

The goat disappeared.

The laugh did not matter anymore.

I had a line.

I said it.

The first set lasted maybe eighteen minutes.

Orin closed with a short piece about a magistrate, a stolen chicken, and
three witnesses who all claimed to be the chicken's owner.

I was not in it.

That gave me time to watch the bowl.

People laughed.

Some paid.

Many did not.

One man watched almost the entire thing, laughed twice, then walked away
carrying a new shovel.

A woman who had arrived halfway through dropped two copper.

A boy dropped a smooth white stone.

I looked at him.

He said, "Lucky."

I left it.

Future money had diversified.

At the end, Teren said, "Thank you."

No request.

No announcement.

No promise of another set.

People broke apart because market people had somewhere else to be.

The half-circle dissolved in less than a minute.

Rinna picked up the bowl.

Teren looked at her.

She counted with one hand inside it.

Marek leaned.

Rinna turned away.

He leaned farther.

"Enough?" Teren asked.

Rinna counted again.

"Fourteen."

Marek said, "Fourteen!"

Rinna said, "You are not helping."

"Fourteen is helping."

Teren looked at the crowd moving through the market.

"Again?"

Rinna looked toward the wagon field.

"Oats already paid."

"Food."

"Yes."

"Dast."

"Maybe."

She handed him the bowl.

"Again."

That was it.

We had earned a second set.

Not much more.

Enough.

Teren said, "Twenty minutes."

Marek said, "Rest?"

"Advertise."

"How?"

"Be visible."

Marek put the crown back on.

"Finally, management recognizes my gifts."

Teren walked away.

The second set was different because the market had changed.

The wool auction had started near the center square.

Half the people who had watched us were gone.

Different people came south.

More traders.

Fewer children.

More people carrying money and less interest in giving it away.

Teren cut the King.

Marek objected.

"No King?"

"No."

"What opens?"

"Shopkeeper."

Marek stared at him.

"I have been replaced by debt."

I said, "Common."

He pointed at me.

"See? He's already working."

Shopkeeper in a livestock market was dangerous because everybody
understood debt.

Iven entered first carrying the old coat.

I followed with the battered table.

The onion woman said, "Him again."

I said, "Unfortunately."

That got three people.

Not enough.

Iven slapped a folded paper on the table.

"I have paid."

"You have presented paper."

"It says paid."

"I can write king."

Marek shouted from behind the wagon, "No."

The crowd laughed.

He was not in the scene.

Teren looked at him.

Marek raised both hands.

Iven said, "You heard the King."

"I heard unemployment."

A cattle seller barked a laugh.

Someone stopped.

Then someone else.

The set built slower.

The first crowd had formed around noise and the goat.

This one formed around people hearing other people laugh.

That took longer.

It also held differently.

A man in a leather apron argued with me from outside the scene.

"If he paid, he's paid."

I said, "You know him?"

"No."

"Then why are you risking your reputation?"

"I don't have one."

"Excellent. Stand for office."

The man laughed.

Iven said, "Can he forgive the debt?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Poor judgment."

The leather-apron man shouted, "I have that!"

"Still no."

Copper hit the bowl.

The second set became better than the first.

Then I ruined part of it.

Not onstage.

Between pieces.

Teren told me, "Take the bowl to Rinna."

I heard, "Take the bowl."

I picked it up.

Rinna was not where she had been.

I carried it behind the wagon looking for her.

A trader immediately shouted, "Where's the bowl?"

I stopped.

The crowd had people reaching for money.

I had removed the thing they were supposed to put it in.

Teren stared at me.

I put it back.

Not where it had been.

The onion woman pointed.

"Cart."

I moved it again.

A cart came through thirty seconds later.

Good.

Rinna found me.

"Why did you move it?"

"Teren."

Teren said, "I said take it to Rinna."

"You weren't there."

Rinna looked at me.

"So you brought it nowhere."

"Yes."

"Useful."

"No."

She took the bowl.

That was the entire review.

Sword came second.

The goat was gone.

Good.

The mounting cloth had a wet chewed corner.

Bad.

Nessa had folded it under so nobody could see.

Pell had moved the board farther from the pen without being told.

Better.

This Sword did not get the goat laugh.

It got something else.

A woman near the front recognized the piece from the first set.

When Serra said, "I require a weapon," the woman quietly said,
"Judgment."

I heard her.

So did Serra.

Serra changed.

"I require a weapon because judgment has failed me."

I said, "Again?"

The woman laughed.

That was enough.

We did not repeat the first exchange.

The scene moved.

A little later a man asked what the Sword cost.

I said, "Depends who is buying."

"Me."

"No."

"Why?"

"You asked."

That worked.

Not huge.

Enough.

The second set ended with Serra and Orin doing a short argument piece I
had never seen before.

Not the widow.

This one involved a landlord, a missing roof tile, and an accusation
that rain was a tenant responsibility.

I watched from the wagon.

Orin was better than me.

Not in a way I could fix by noticing.

He could let silence sit until the crowd leaned toward him.

Then Serra would cut it.

They had done this before.

Probably many times.

I watched.

A man beside me said, "You with them?"

"Apparently."

"Where next?"

I looked east.

"Maybe Dast."

"Fair?"

"Maybe."

He nodded.

"Good fair."

"You've been?"

"Every year."

That got my attention.

"Covered market?"

"Some."

"Performance?"

He looked at me.

"I sell harness."

"Right."

He pointed east.

"If you're going, don't take north ford. Bridge at Lerren's faster this
week."

"Why?"

"Ford deep."

Davin needed that.

I found him after the set.

He listened.

"Who?"

"Harness seller."

"Name?"

I looked back.

The man was gone.

"I don't know."

Davin stared.

"He sells harness."

"Good."

That was not praise.

The second collection was better.

Rinna counted twenty-one copper.

Thirty-five total.

Plus one smooth stone.

Marek held up the stone.

"Reserve."

"Put it down," Rinna said.

He did.

Thirty-five copper was not a hall gate.

It was not private silver.

It was more than six.

It was enough that nobody looked angry about staying.

Teren paid the performers who had worked both sets.

I got two copper.

Marek got one.

He stared at it.

"Why one?"

"You weren't in second."

"I advertised."

"You shouted once."

"Royal marketing."

"One."

Serra got two.

Iven two.

Orin two.

Other shares moved through Rinna's hands. Pell got something for work.
Nessa did. Davin did not ask in front of me.

The company kept the rest.

Rinna counted it again, then put it away.

"Food," she said.

Teren nodded.

"Dast?"

"Still possible."

The word had changed.

Not confirmed.

Possible.

A woman from the market committee found Teren while we were packing.

Not to pay us.

To tell us we had left the south edge clean.

Teren said, "Good."

She said, "If you're back next month, ask before market week."

"Why?"

"Cheaper rooms."

Then she left.

That was as close as Kest came to inviting us back.

The onion woman sold Rinna a sack of onions for road food.

Not free.

A little cheaper because the market was ending and she did not want to
carry them home.

Soft economy could apparently include not wanting to lift onions twice.

Pell tried to buy the lucky stone from the bowl.

"It isn't ours?" he asked.

"It was given."

"Then ours."

"Why would you buy it?"

"Accounting."

Rinna gave him the stone.

He put it in his pocket.

"Profit."

Nobody stopped him.

By late afternoon, the livestock market had started taking itself apart.

Pens emptied.

Animals left.

Temporary awnings folded.

The assembly room was filling for supper we were not attending.

Noll stood in the doorway directing tables.

He saw Teren.

"Eight."

Teren said, "No."

Noll nodded.

Apparently their negotiation had survived the day.

We did not stay another night.

That mattered.

Kest had paid enough to justify the morning.

Not enough to justify buying another Kest evening.

Rinna bought bread and cheap dried meat.

Davin watered the horses.

We loaded.

The long box went last.

Upright.

Dry.

Davin tied it.

Nobody cared.

Teren stood beside Rinna with the folded paper from Lady Merra's dinner
guest.

"Dast," he said.

"Six days became?"

"Four from here if road holds."

Davin said, "Three and half."

Rinna looked at him.

"With what road?"

"Bridge."

I said, "Lerren's."

Davin looked at me.

I explained the harness seller.

He asked the name.

"I still don't know."

"Ford?"

"Deep."

Davin nodded once.

Apparently anonymous harness information had passed inspection.

Rinna said, "Fair still no guarantee."

Teren said, "No."

"Covered market?"

"Possible."

"Contact?"

"Card says ask for Bellan."

"Answer?"

"No."

Marek climbed onto the wagon.

"We try."

Rinna looked at him.

"Don't."

He smiled.

Teren looked east.

Then at the money Rinna had put away.

Then at the road.

"Dast."

That was the decision.

Not because Kest had been good.

Because Kest had been enough.

We rolled out while the market was still disappearing behind us.

I sat with my crutches tied beside the wagon and two new copper in my
purse.

The brass clasp stayed in my inner pocket.

Carrow was west.

Lyssa was west.

Hessa was west.

Dast was east.

I knew all of that.

The road bent.

Kest vanished behind cattle pens and evening dust.

Nobody asked when I was going home.

Neither did I.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 166

## THE ROADHAND

We left Kest with onions.

That was what the market became once the cattle, noise, collection bowl,
goat, and thirty-five copper were behind us. A sack of onions sat
beneath the wagon seat. Bread was wrapped beside it. The dried meat had
been divided into pieces that looked insufficient before anybody ate
them.

Marek looked into the food sack.

"Is there cheese?"

Rinna said, "No."

"Was there cheese?"

"No."

"Could there have been cheese?"

"Yes."

He looked wounded by possibility.

The road east was crowded enough that we did not feel alone for the
first hour. Market carts went both directions. Empty livestock wagons
rattled west. A family with three children and a cage of chickens passed
us, then stopped to fix a strap, then passed us again. Two men driving
sheep occupied the center of the road with the calm certainty of people
who knew everyone else would move.

Davin moved.

The wagons did not move quickly.

By evening, Kest had stopped existing behind us.

Not literally.

Probably.

I could no longer see anything that belonged to it.

We camped beside a low stand of trees where somebody had camped before
us and left a black circle of old fire stones. Davin checked the ground
before committing the wagons. Rinna checked the water. Teren checked the
folded card again.

I watched everybody check things and then carried the onion sack to the
wrong wagon.

Nessa said, "Why?"

"Food."

"Not here."

"Right."

I carried it back.

That was my contribution to logistics.

Dinner was bread, dried meat, onion, and water.

Marek held a piece of onion between two fingers.

"This is punishment."

"You wanted food," Rinna said.

"I wanted dinner."

"You have dinner."

"This is components."

Orin ate his.

Serra ate hers.

I ate mine.

Marek looked around for support.

Pell said, "I like onions."

"Of course you do."

Pell had the wooden fish beside him and the white stone from Kest
balanced on its back.

Marek pointed.

"That has more wealth than I do."

"It's lucky," Pell said.

"Sell it."

"No."

"Then it isn't wealth."

Pell considered this and put the stone in his pocket.

Nobody performed.

Nobody rehearsed.

After dark, Nessa worked on the chewed mounting cloth by firelight until
she decided firelight was making the color worse and stopped. Pell held
the damaged corner while she folded it.

"Goat," he said.

"I know."

"It could have been worse."

Nessa looked at him.

Pell reconsidered.

"It was exactly as bad as it was."

"Better."

Serra wrote something with the paper braced against her knee. I did not
ask what. Orin disappeared beyond the trees for long enough that I
noticed and not long enough that anybody else appeared concerned.

Marek told Iven a story about a baron who had once paid him three silver
to insult a cousin.

Iven said, "No."

"You weren't there."

"Neither were you."

"I was central."

"To a story you invented."

"That is what central means."

I lay down beneath the wagon.

The road had been quiet for almost an hour.

I could still hear one of the horses tearing grass.

No audience.

No mill wheel.

No market bell.

No money hitting a bowl.

Just people sleeping because there was another road tomorrow.

That was work too, apparently.

Nobody paid for it.

In the morning Davin asked, "Bridge?"

I was eating the last heel of yesterday's bread.

"Lerren's?"

He waited.

"Apparently."

He nodded.

That was the entire reward for remembering useful information.

The road split before noon.

The left branch went north toward the ford. The right dropped through a
shallow valley toward a line of trees and a stone marker whose lettering
had been repaired often enough that the newer cuts did not quite match
the old ones.

LERREN 3.

Someone had scratched FORD BAD beneath it.

Davin got down from the wagon and looked at the ruts.

Teren said, "Bridge?"

Davin said, "Bridge."

Nobody asked me.

That seemed reasonable.

Traffic thickened as we approached the river. Not fair traffic yet.
Ordinary bridge traffic. Grain carts. A wagon carrying clay jars packed
in straw. Two riders. A farmer with a pig tied in a small cart who spent
most of the queue telling the pig to stop doing something the pig
continued doing.

The bridge sat between two low stone abutments. Timber span. Narrow
enough that wagons crossed one direction at a time.

I looked at it.

Teren said, "Don't."

"I'm sitting."

"You can lean sitting."

"I've been told."

There was a toll shed.

Of course there was.

Rinna climbed down before we reached it.

"How much?" Marek asked.

"Company."

"That is not a number."

"It is the number that doesn't concern you."

The toll keeper counted wagons, horses, and people with less interest in
us than the Kest goat had shown. He looked at my crutches tied beside
me.

"Passenger?"

Before I could answer, Teren said, "Player."

The keeper marked something on a slate.

"Same."

Apparently my professional identity had achieved administrative equality
with sitting down.

Rinna paid several copper.

I did not see exactly how many.

The gate lifted.

The bridge took us.

The river below was high and brown enough that I understood the harness
seller's opinion of the ford without needing to see it. Branches moved
in the current. The horses disliked the hollow sound of wheels over
timber but kept going.

Halfway across, I looked downstream.

No mystery.

No broken support.

No secret.

Just water going somewhere else faster than we were.

On the far side, a woman selling apples from a cart had positioned
herself where everybody who had just paid a toll could immediately spend
more money.

I respected that.

I bought one apple for myself.

One copper got me two because one had a bruise.

I ate the good one while walking beside the wagon.

The bruised one went into my pocket.

Marek saw it.

"Second apple?"

"Yes."

"You've changed."

"I bought fruit."

"Exactly."

He held out his hand.

"No."

"Capital is trapped."

"Good."

"You don't understand finance."

"I understand this apple."

I ate it later too.

Lerren itself was barely a settlement. Bridge, toll shed, smith, inn,
stable yard, six or seven houses, and a shrine set back from the road
under trees. It existed because the river made people stop.

We stopped.

Not to perform.

The innkeeper did not know us.

The stable boy did not know us.

The woman carrying buckets through the yard did not know us and became
annoyed when I stood where she needed to walk.

"Move."

I moved.

"Other way."

I moved the other way.

"Thank you."

That was the whole interaction.

It was refreshing.

Davin wanted one horse checked because a shoe had started wearing
unevenly. The smith looked at it, looked at Davin, and said, "Tomorrow
if you want iron."

Davin said, "No."

The smith shrugged.

"Then next town."

Davin checked the hoof himself.

I asked, "Bad?"

"No."

"Then why check?"

He looked at me.

"Because."

Good.

Rinna paid for water and a small measure of oats. Teren asked the
innkeeper about the east road.

The innkeeper said, "Fair?"

"Dast."

"Then everybody's going."

"Road?"

"Dry enough. North side after the old orchard."

Davin said, "Why?"

"South shoulder washed last spring."

"Still?"

"Still."

Teren looked at me.

I said, "I didn't know that."

"No one expected you to."

It should not have sounded reassuring.

It did.

We stayed long enough to rest the horses and eat.

No room.

No performance.

No one asked what was in the wagons.

A little boy stared at the Sword mounting board until Pell told him it
was a table.

The boy said, "Bad table."

Pell said, "Yes."

Apparently criticism was becoming consistent across regions.

Serra sat alone behind the stable for part of the stop with folded paper
in her hand. She did not write while I could see her. She just read.

Orin bought something from the smith.

Small.

Wrapped in cloth.

It went into the same sort of private space his other things went.

Nobody asked.

I was beginning to understand that traveling with people did not mean
eventually receiving an explanation for everything they did.

It mostly meant being nearby while they continued doing it.

We left Lerren after midday.

The road beyond the river was quieter for several miles.

Then the fair began arriving from the opposite direction.

Not the fair itself.

Pieces.

A wagon stacked with painted wooden bowls.

A woman driving two mules with bundles of dyed cloth.

Three men walking beside a cart full of iron pans.

A family carrying poles that might become an awning.

Two musicians with narrow cases strapped to their backs.

Marek turned around to watch them.

"Competition."

One of the musicians heard him.

"From you?"

Marek put a hand to his chest.

The man kept walking.

Serra laughed.

"Brutal."

"I wasn't ready."

"Apparently neither is Dast."

More wagons appeared as the afternoon went on.

Some were going toward the fair.

Some were leaving nearby villages to sell there.

At a roadside well, a woman told Rinna that bread would cost more in
Dast by tomorrow.

Rinna bought two loaves from her.

Marek said, "We have bread."

"Now we have cheaper bread."

"That is almost investment."

Rinna looked at him.

He went away.

By the second night, road food had become road food.

Bread.

Onion.

Meat.

Water.

The new loaf was softer than the old one.

That was the event.

Pell dealt cards on an overturned crate after dinner. Iven played. Marek
watched for a while and did not join.

"You have money," I said.

"Exactly."

"You're learning?"

"Don't insult me."

He went to sleep with his copper intact.

I lost one hand to Pell and won the next.

No money.

The stakes were who had to refill the water pot.

I lost overall.

That cost walking.

I carried the pot carefully because spilling it would mean doing the
walk again.

On the way back, I passed Teren and Rinna talking beside the lead wagon.

"Bellan," Rinna said.

"If he's there."

"If he isn't?"

"Find whoever is."

"And if there's no space?"

"Find out before unloading."

"Dast prices?"

"We don't stay in town unless the work pays."

Davin sat on the wagon tongue repairing a leather strap.

"Two days," he said.

Teren looked at him.

"To Dast?"

"Edge."

"Fair?"

"Traffic."

That was close enough.

I brought the water back.

Pell said, "Took you long enough."

I set it beside him.

"Drink less."

He drank.

The next morning we joined a line of wagons without deciding to.

There were simply enough of them going east that our speed became their
speed.

A cart ahead of us carried carved spoons.

The wagon behind us carried three enormous pumpkins and one old woman
who stared at everybody like she suspected theft.

At midday, the road climbed.

From the ridge I could see more country east than I had expected.

Fields.

Low woods.

A pale line of road.

Smoke from two settlements.

Farther away, another road meeting ours.

Wagons on it.

All moving the same general direction.

Dast was not visible.

That made it worse somehow.

Or better.

I could not tell.

I had left Carrow to travel with the company.

That had been true.

I had gone to the eastern town.

Also true.

Then north.

Then private work.

Then a market.

Then a mill.

Then Kest.

Each place had been close enough to the place before it that I had never
needed to decide what the whole thing was.

One more show.

One more road.

One more morning.

Now I could not point west and pretend Carrow was just beyond the next
hill.

Lyssa might already have my letter.

She might have written back.

If she had, the reply had nowhere to find me unless she guessed better
than I had planned.

Hessa expected me back.

Not today.

I had never said today.

That was convenient.

I touched the inside of my coat where the brass clasp was wrapped.

Serra was sitting across from me.

She noticed.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

She looked back at the road.

I almost asked whether she was going to Dast because she wanted to.

That would have been a stupid question.

She was already going.

So was I.

At the next stop, Teren handed me a bucket.

"Water."

"Where?"

He pointed toward a farmyard well.

"Ask."

I went.

The farmer charged nothing for water but told me not to use the first
trough because it was for calves.

I had already started toward the first trough.

"Other one."

"Right."

"Players?"

I looked back at the wagons.

"Yes."

"Dast?"

"Yes."

It came out before I thought about it.

Not maybe.

Not apparently.

Yes.

The farmer nodded.

"Busy."

"Good?"

He shrugged.

"For somebody."

I filled the bucket.

On the way back, I realized that was the first time I had told a
stranger where we were going without checking whether the company had
changed its mind.

Teren took the bucket.

"Thanks."

That was all.

We camped that night beside three other fair wagons.

One sold pottery.

One carried preserved fruit.

The third belonged to four people with painted poles, rolled canvas, and
a dog that could stand on its back legs for an unsettling amount of
time.

Marek watched the dog.

"Competition."

The dog's owner said, "He works cheaper."

Marek looked offended.

The owner fed the dog.

No one performed.

The painted-pole people did not ask us to perform.

We did not ask them.

They repaired canvas.

Nessa repaired cloth.

Davin checked wheels.

Rinna counted food.

Teren talked briefly with one of the pottery sellers about the road
ahead.

Pell tried to make the wooden fish bite the white stone and failed.

The dog watched him.

I sat against the wagon wheel and ate bread and onion.

The eastern sky went dark slowly.

Somewhere beyond the next ridges, people were building a harvest fair.

We would reach its outer traffic tomorrow.

Maybe Bellan would be there.

Maybe there would be work.

Maybe there would be nowhere to sleep.

Nobody knew.

For the first time, that did not feel like a gap in the plan.

It was the plan.

Davin walked past me.

"Up early."

"How early?"

"Early."

"Helpful."

He kept walking.

I looked west once.

There was nothing to see.

Then I got under the wagon and went to sleep.

The morning after Lerren also taught me that company work could be
assigned before I was fully awake.

Rinna kicked the sole of my boot.

"Up."

"I am."

"You are horizontal."

"Temporary."

She handed me a coil of cord.

"What?"

"Rear cover."

I crawled out and found one corner of the wagon cover hanging loose
where the knot had worked itself ugly during the night. Davin was
already with the horses. Pell was somewhere under the other wagon.
Nobody explained why the cord had come to me.

I tied what I thought was the right knot.

Rinna looked at it.

"No."

I untied it.

"Why?"

"Because Davin will cut it off and then look at me."

"Terrible."

"Yes."

She showed me which loop she wanted once, then left before I had
finished.

The second attempt held.

Davin checked it later without comment.

That felt dangerously close to approval, so I did not mention it.

At another farm stop, I carried a bucket and a sack of oats at the same
time because I did not want to make two trips. This was a poor decision
with crutches. I got halfway across the yard, put the oats down, carried
the water, came back for the oats, and discovered Marek sitting on the
sack.

"Move."

"I'm guarding it."

"From what?"

He looked around the empty yard.

"Success."

I pushed his knee with the end of one crutch.

He moved.

The farmer's wife watched us from the doorway without any sign that she
knew or cared that either of us had stood in front of crowds the day
before.

"Players," she said eventually.

Marek brightened.

Then she pointed at the wagon.

"Keep that wheel off my herb bed."

Davin had already done so.

Marek's brightness faded.

"She recognized us."

"She recognized wheels."

"Same profession."

It was not.

We loaded the oats and left.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 167

## THE APPLICANT

Davin's early turned out to mean before the dog woke up.

The dog belonged to the people with the painted poles. It was asleep
beneath their wagon when Rinna kicked my boot.

"Up."

"I've heard this one."

"Then improve."

Around us, the fair road was already beginning to move. The pottery
wagon had gone. The preserved-fruit people were tying their last cover.
Somebody farther down the camp lane had a fire going and was burning
breakfast badly enough that the smoke tasted bitter.

We ate standing.

Bread.

Onion.

A little dried meat.

Marek held his piece of onion up to the gray morning.

"Still components."

"No one promised transformation," Serra said.

"Cooking exists."

"So does money."

He ate the onion.

The painted-pole people were packing their canvas. Their dog woke,
stretched, and stood on its back legs against the wagon wheel while one
of them tied a bundle overhead.

Marek pointed.

"Show-off."

The owner said, "He has breakfast."

Marek stopped pointing.

Davin had the horses ready before the rest of us had finished
swallowing. I carried water to the rear wagon, put the bucket where
Rinna had shown me yesterday, and checked the cover knot without being
asked.

It was still holding.

I did not tell anyone.

The road east collected wagons by the mile.

At first there were six of us moving in roughly the same direction. Then
twelve. Then enough that passing became an argument. Farmers drove carts
loaded with squash and apples. A wagon of barrels smelled sharply of
vinegar. A woman walked beside three geese tied together by their feet,
which seemed unfair but effective. Men with rolled carpets sat on top of
them like minor kings.

Temporary signs began appearing at forks.

DAST FAIR.

WAGON FIELD.

STOCK EAST.

TRADERS SOUTH.

One sign said ENTERTAINERS and pointed left.

Marek sat straighter.

"Finally."

Davin kept right.

Marek looked at him.

"Entertainers."

"Old sign," Davin said.

The arrow had been crossed out lower down in charcoal.

Beneath it somebody had written WEST FIELD FULL.

Marek sat back.

"Insulting."

"Accurate," Rinna said.

We had not seen Dast yet.

We saw its parking problem.

Fields on both sides of the road had been divided with rope, stakes,
painted boards, and people holding sticks. Wagons turned off in lines.
Some were waved through. Some were stopped. A man in a yellow cap
shouted at a cart carrying pumpkins until the driver shouted back that
he had been told east.

"Not this east!"

"How many easts do you have?"

"Today? Four!"

That did not help me.

The company reached a fork where three fair workers were sorting
traffic.

One pointed at us.

"Trade?"

Teren said, "Players."

The worker pointed left.

Another worker immediately shouted, "Not left!"

The first one shouted, "They moved players?"

"Yesterday!"

"Where?"

"South three!"

The first worker looked at Teren.

"South three."

"Where's that?"

"Past grain. Before stock."

"Which grain?"

The worker had already turned to a cheese wagon.

We continued.

Marek said, "Organized."

Rinna said, "Very."

Davin said nothing.

He found south three.

I would not have.

The field was beyond two grain yards, behind a row of temporary horse
pens, and marked by a board whose THREE had been painted over a TWO.
Half the field was already full.

A woman at the entrance held out her hand.

"Token."

Teren gave her Bellan's card.

She looked at it.

"Not a token."

"We're looking for Bellan."

"So is everyone."

"Players."

"I can see."

She looked at me, then at Marek's crown case, then at the Sword board.

"Two wagons?"

"Yes."

"One night?"

"Depends."

"Then one night."

Rinna said, "Cost?"

"Four copper for wagons. Water at trough. Horses separate."

"How separate?"

"Ask horses."

Rinna waited.

The woman sighed.

"Stable office."

"Can we hold without paying?"

"No."

Teren looked at Rinna.

Rinna looked at the field.

"Four."

She paid.

The woman handed Teren a flat wooden token marked S3-41.

"Keep that visible. No fires after dark. No dumping wash water in the
lane. No animals tied to the rope. If you block the grain wagons, they
will move you."

"Who?"

"Grain wagons."

That seemed sufficient.

Davin drove us to forty-one.

I saw a patch of grass beside the rope and pointed.

"That?"

"No," Davin said.

"Why?"

"Turn."

I looked.

The wagon needed room to turn.

"Right."

He put us where we belonged.

By the time the horses were unhitched, Teren and Rinna were already
leaving.

"Bellan," Teren said.

Rinna pointed at me.

"Stay."

"I was going to."

"Good."

Apparently my first job in Dast was not getting lost.

I watched the wagons.

That lasted eleven minutes.

Then Nessa handed me a bundle of cloth and said, "Hold."

I held it.

Pell disappeared beneath the rear wagon.

Davin went to the stable office.

Serra left without telling me where she was going.

Orin left in a different direction.

Marek stood in the lane wearing his good coat despite the dust.

"Where are you going?"

"To assess the field."

"You're wearing the coat."

"Exactly."

"Don't spend your copper."

He looked offended.

"I have discipline."

"Recent discipline."

"Still counts."

He walked away.

I held cloth.

The fair moved around us.

South three was not an entertainment camp.

It was overflow.

Two musicians occupied a wagon three spaces down. A family with a puppet
booth was across the lane. The painted-pole people with the dog arrived
twenty minutes after us and were assigned near the far rope. The dog
recognized nobody and seemed fine with that.

Beyond the field, the fair itself kept making noise without showing me
much of itself.

Hammers.

Animals.

Bells.

Someone testing a horn.

Someone else shouting numbers.

Wagon wheels.

A burst of cheering from somewhere west.

Then nothing.

Pell emerged.

"What are you doing?"

"Holding."

"Why?"

"Nessa."

He nodded.

That explained everything.

She returned and took the cloth.

"Good."

"What was it?"

"Clean."

"Still?"

She inspected the edge.

"Mostly."

That was apparently success.

Davin came back with stable terms.

Rinna was not there.

Teren was not there.

He told Nessa instead.

"Too much."

Nessa said, "How much?"

He told her quietly.

She made a face.

"Water?"

"Free."

"Oats?"

"No."

"Of course."

Davin looked at me.

"Rear wheel."

"What?"

"Watch."

He lifted one side of the wagon with a short jack and crawled near the
hub.

I watched.

Not the wheel.

The lane.

That took me a moment.

A grain wagon came through five minutes later, wide enough that its
driver swore at the puppet family for leaving a stool too far out.

I moved our stool before he reached us.

The driver did not notice.

That felt like a very small promotion.

Teren returned alone.

"No Bellan?" Nessa asked.

"Found his table."

"Not him?"

"Found his assistant."

"Not Bellan."

"No."

"Where's Rinna?"

"Prices."

That could mean anything.

Teren took the card from his pocket.

"Bellan is in the covered market until noon, then east judging yard,
then apparently nowhere anyone can promise."

"Useful," I said.

"Come."

I looked at the wagon.

"Davin said watch."

Davin, still under it, said, "Go."

Fine.

Teren and I went looking for a man who was apparently everywhere except
where we were.

The fair became visible by pieces.

First produce.

Long rows of apples, squash, beans, onions, dried herbs, honey, grain,
flour, cider, preserves. Then tools. Then cloth. Then animals again.
Every lane had its own traffic. Every crossing had somebody who knew
which carts were allowed through and assumed I did too.

I followed Teren.

At the first covered lane, I stepped across a painted white line.

A woman carrying a crate said, "Out."

I moved.

Teren kept walking.

"What?"

"Loading."

"How do you know?"

"She said out."

"Before that."

"I didn't."

Good.

We passed the musicians from the road.

They had a real pitch now beneath a striped awning. One played a fiddle.
The other played a small drum with one hand and collected with the
other. They were good.

Not interestingly good.

Just good.

People stopped.

A woman dropped copper without being asked.

Marek was standing ten feet away watching them.

He saw us.

"Research."

Teren said, "Move."

Marek moved.

A puppet booth farther on had children packed three rows deep. The
puppeteer was doing two voices at once while another person changed
figures behind the cloth.

I stopped.

Teren did not.

I caught up.

"You've never seen puppets?" he asked.

"Not those."

"What about them?"

"The hands."

"Later."

That was fair.

The covered market was not one building.

It was a long roofed trading hall with open sides, stone columns, raised
loading edges, and permanent stalls along the center. Harvest fair had
filled every gap.

Cheese.

Smoked meat.

Baskets.

Seed.

Tools.

A knife seller.

A woman selling painted tiles.

At the south end, a square of floor had been left open between columns.

A comic pair were using it.

No scenery.

One bench.

Two people.

A crowd on three sides.

They were arguing over a dead goose that neither of them wanted to admit
owning.

The shorter performer said, "It followed you."

The taller one said, "So did my wife. I deny both."

The crowd broke.

Teren stopped.

So did I.

The pair were better at the space than I would have been.

They knew exactly how far they could turn before one side lost the face.
They kept the bench angled. When a handcart needed through behind them,
the taller performer moved half a step without looking and the cart
passed.

Nobody applauded the movement.

Nobody noticed.

That was probably why it worked.

A woman with a ledger stood near one of the columns watching both the
act and the lane.

Teren approached her.

"Bellan?"

"Not me."

"Where?"

"Judging yard."

"I was told noon."

"It's noon."

I looked up.

There was no useful clock in the roof.

Apparently noon had happened while we watched a dead goose.

Teren showed her the card.

She read it.

"Merra house."

"Yes."

"You're late."

"We didn't have a booking."

"Then you're not late."

"Helpful."

She handed the card back.

"Bellan's at east judging. If he isn't, try the entertainment board."

"Where?"

"North arch."

"Which is?"

She pointed.

"Thank you."

"Don't thank me yet."

We found Bellan beside six pigs.

Not judging them.

Arguing about a singer.

He was a narrow man in a brown coat with fair dust on the hem and a
strip of blue cloth tied around one arm. His hair had gone mostly gray.
He held three folded schedules and one half-eaten pear.

A woman in a green dress was saying, "She has the west platform at
fourth bell."

Bellan said, "She has west platform if the grain speeches end."

"They won't."

"Then she doesn't."

"You promised."

"I scheduled."

"Same thing."

"Not at a fair."

The woman left angry.

Bellan took a bite of pear.

Teren waited.

Bellan looked at him.

"Who?"

Teren gave him the card.

Bellan read it while chewing.

"Right."

That was all.

No recognition.

No delight.

No immediate money.

"You're the Carrow company?"

"East Market."

"How many?"

"Depends on piece."

"How many mouths?"

Rinna would have liked that question.

"Twelve traveling."

Bellan looked at the wagons in the distance as if he could see them
through three buildings.

"Horses?"

"Yes."

"Room?"

"Work first."

"Good."

He unfolded one schedule.

"Covered market is full."

Teren said nothing.

"West platform is full."

Nothing.

"South yard is livestock until tomorrow afternoon."

"Then?"

"Mess."

"East?"

"Local dancing."

"Evening?"

"Paid singers."

"Tomorrow?"

"Depends what breaks."

Teren looked at the schedule.

"What do you have?"

Bellan looked at him for the first time like that was the correct
question.

"North arcade. First bell after noon. Twenty minutes."

"Guarantee?"

"No."

"Collection?"

"Allowed."

"Space fee?"

"No."

"Food?"

"No."

"Lodging?"

"No."

Teren's face did not change.

Bellan continued.

"If you draw, I can give you a second slot at fourth bell near the cider
yard."

"Can?"

"If the puppet people don't extend."

"Guarantee?"

"No."

"Anything guaranteed?"

Bellan took another bite of pear.

"Roof if it rains sideways."

Teren looked toward the covered market.

"North arcade is covered?"

"Mostly."

"Mostly?"

"Depends on wind."

I liked him less than Vessa.

Teren said, "Why would I stay?"

Bellan shrugged.

"Because tomorrow has twice today's crowd."

"That's not pay."

"No."

"Merra's man said fair work."

"Merra's man had dinner."

That was good enough that Teren almost smiled.

Almost.

Bellan looked past us.

"Can you stop people?"

Teren said, "Sometimes."

"What do you do?"

"Mixed pieces."

"Music?"

"No."

"Animals?"

"No."

"Fire?"

"No."

"Good. No fire."

He looked at me.

"What does he do?"

Teren said, "Sword."

Bellan looked at my missing leg, then my crutches.

"Actual?"

"No."

"Good."

Apparently this was the second most important safety question.

Bellan folded the schedule.

"North arcade. Tomorrow. First bell after noon. Twenty minutes.
Collection. If it works, find me."

"And if it doesn't?"

"Don't."

Teren held out his hand.

Bellan looked at it.

"For what?"

"Slot."

"You have it."

"Token?"

"No."

"Schedule?"

"I wrote it."

"Where?"

Bellan tapped the paper.

Teren lowered his hand.

"Fine."

Bellan turned toward someone shouting his name.

"Wait."

Teren stopped.

Bellan pointed at me.

"Can he get up three steps?"

I said, "Probably."

Teren said, "Where?"

"North arcade."

"Ramp?"

"No."

"Then no."

Bellan looked at me again.

"Three low steps."

Teren said, "No."

I said, "I can do three steps."

Teren looked at me.

"I can."

"With board?"

"No."

"Then no."

Bellan scratched something on the schedule.

"South end of arcade. Loading slope."

Teren nodded.

"That works."

It was the first accommodation of the negotiation and it happened
because there was a loading slope.

Not because anyone cared about me.

I liked that.

We walked back toward south three.

Teren said, "Don't promise stairs."

"I didn't promise."

"You said probably."

"That's not promise."

"It is to people with schedules."

"Fine."

We found Rinna halfway back carrying a small sack of oats and looking
offended by it.

"How bad?" Teren asked.

"Bad."

"Work?"

"Tomorrow. North arcade. Twenty. Collection."

"Guarantee?"

"No."

"No food?"

"No."

"No lodging?"

"No."

Rinna stared at him.

"That's Kest with more expensive oats."

"More people."

"More people don't eat oats."

"Some pay."

"Some don't."

"Yes."

She shifted the sack.

"Second slot?"

"If first draws."

"Where?"

"Cider yard."

"Better?"

"Probably."

Rinna looked at me.

I said, "I didn't say it."

"Good."

We returned to the wagons.

Marek was gone.

Nessa was angry about dust.

Davin had finished the wheel.

Pell had acquired a paper cone of something fried and refused to say
where.

Serra was back and had a strip of red thread tied around one finger for
no reason I knew.

Orin was still absent.

The dog act was setting painted poles in the far corner of south three.

Their owner saw us.

"Got work?"

Teren said, "Tomorrow."

"Where?"

"North arcade."

The man winced.

Marek appeared behind him.

"Why?"

"Wind."

Teren looked at Bellan's schedule in his hand.

"Mostly covered."

The dog owner laughed.

"Mostly."

Marek looked delighted.

"We have a room."

"No," Teren said.

"We have an arcade."

"Mostly."

"Roof."

"Sometimes."

"Professional."

Rinna dropped the oats beside Davin.

"We are paying to stay tonight."

That quieted Marek.

"How much?"

"Enough."

Teren said, "One night."

Rinna looked at him.

"If tomorrow pays."

"If tomorrow pays."

There it was again.

Not a booking.

Not really.

A place to try.

The fair had not hired us.

It had made room for us to ask strangers for money under a roof that
apparently depended on wind.

I sat on the wagon step.

Across the field, the puppet family was hanging painted cloth. Beyond
them, the dog stood on its back legs while a child clapped.

Somewhere in the fair, musicians were already earning.

The comic pair had a crowd.

The singers had an evening guarantee.

We had tomorrow after noon.

Twenty minutes.

I reached into my coat and touched the wrapped brass clasp.

Dast had a courier row. I had seen the sign near the north arch.

I could write Lyssa tomorrow.

Maybe.

First we had to earn tomorrow.

Teren pointed at me.

"North arcade in the morning."

"Why?"

"Look at the slope."

"I thought you already did."

"I looked at Bellan."

"Different."

"Very."

I nodded.

Apparently I had applied for work and received an inspection.

That was close enough.

Behind us, somebody shouted that a wagon was in the wrong lane.

Three people shouted different answers.

Dast continued without waiting for us.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 168

## THE PITCHMAN

The north arcade had more wind than roof.

That was my professional assessment.

I arrived before breakfast with Pell, the Sword board, and instructions
from Teren to find out whether the loading slope worked. Pell carried
one end of the board. I carried the other badly until we reached the
first patch of churned ground, then we stopped pretending and dragged it
on its edge.

Dast was already awake.

Someone had washed the stone lane and pushed yesterday's cabbage leaves
into a wet pile beside a drain. Produce wagons backed toward the covered
market. A boy carried six empty baskets at once because apparently
making two trips was forbidden. Two women were fastening painted cloth
over a honey stall while arguing about whose sister had lied to whom.

The wind lifted one corner of their cloth.

One woman slapped it down without interrupting the argument.

At the north arcade, three carts were already using our performance
space.

Not parked in it.

Using it.

The arcade ran along the north side of the trading hall, roofed in tile
and open toward a lane wide enough for carts. Stone columns held the
roof. Between them, wind came straight through the fair. The south end
had the loading slope Bellan had mentioned, a broad stone incline
leading from the lane to the raised arcade floor.

I looked at the slope.

Pell looked at me.

"Well?"

"I can get up it."

"Good."

"Board can too."

"Good."

"We're done."

A man pushing a handcart up the slope said, "No."

We moved.

He passed us with two crates of turnips.

"What?" I asked.

"Loading."

"I know."

"Then don't stand there."

"We're performing here."

"When?"

"First bell after noon."

He shrugged.

"Then don't stand there now."

Fair.

Pell leaned the board against a column.

The man stopped.

"Not there either."

"Why?"

"Cheese."

I looked.

The stall behind the column had a painted board reading HARRA'S NORTH
FARM CHEESE. A woman inside was stacking pale wheels on cloth.

"That's my column," she said.

Pell moved the board.

"Do you own the roof?"

"Today."

"How much?"

She pointed farther down.

"Ask Bellan if you want to buy weather."

We moved again.

The south end of the arcade gave us enough room for the Sword board,
maybe eight performers, and an audience that would have to choose
between watching us and continuing toward onions.

The wind came through from the lane, struck the wall behind us, and
found new directions.

Pell's coat flapped.

A scrap of paper skittered past.

He caught it with his boot.

"Bad."

"Mostly covered."

He laughed.

We tested the board on the slope.

Up was easy enough with two people.

Turning it at the top was not.

The raised edge left less room than it had looked like from below. I
tried to pivot backward and nearly put my crutch through a basket of
leeks.

A woman slapped my crutch aside with a bunch of greens.

"Not those."

"Sorry."

"Those are paid for."

"They're still here."

"Paid for."

I moved.

Pell said, "You almost bought leeks."

"I don't want leeks."

"Then good save."

The loading man came back down with the empty cart.

I asked, "Do carts keep using this after noon?"

He looked at me as if I had asked whether gravity had afternoon hours.

"Yes."

"During performances?"

"During loading."

"Which is during performances."

"If you're performing during loading."

"Bellan gave us this."

"Bellan doesn't move turnips."

That seemed important.

"How often?"

"Carts?"

"Yes."

"Depends."

"On?"

"Turnips."

He pushed away.

Pell said, "Helpful."

"Very."

We found a place for the board against the rear wall where it would not
block the cheese woman, the leeks, or the loading slope.

Then the wind pushed it over.

Not all the way.

Enough.

Pell caught it.

"More helpful."

We took it back down.

At camp, Teren was eating bread.

"Well?"

"Slope works."

"Good."

"Carts use it."

"During?"

"Everything."

He chewed.

"Space?"

"Enough if we don't own any of it."

"Normal."

"Wind."

"I heard."

"Board needs tying or someone holding it."

Davin, beside the rear wagon, said, "Tie."

Nessa said, "Not cloth."

Nobody had asked her.

She was right.

Pell said, "Rope."

Davin gave him rope.

Apparently inspection was complete.

Breakfast cost company food.

Rinna had bought eggs from somewhere, but not enough eggs to make eggs a
major event. We each got one with bread. Marek looked at his.

"Protein."

I said, "Investment?"

He pointed the egg at me.

"Growth."

"Of what?"

"Potential."

He ate it.

Orin had returned sometime before I woke. His bruise had gone yellow at
the edges. Nobody mentioned where he had been. Serra still had the red
thread around one finger. She used that hand to peel her egg.

Teren explained the set while we ate.

"King first. Short."

Marek nodded.

"Sword."

I nodded.

"Then widow."

Orin looked up.

"Here?"

"Yes."

"Wind."

"Better than death."

"Everything is."

Serra said, "Not everything."

Orin considered.

"Most."

No Shopkeeper.

No Advocate.

Iven was collection.

Pell was props and board.

Nessa immediately said the red overskirt was not going anywhere near the
loading slope.

Serra said, "Good."

Marek said, "My coat?"

Nessa looked at him.

"My coat is fine."

"It will be if you stop touching it."

He stopped.

We carried only what we needed.

That was still too much.

The fair had thickened by the time we returned. The arcade lane was full
of people moving in both directions. Buyers stopped at cheese, honey,
tools, cloth. Children moved against traffic because children were
apparently exempt from roads. The musicians had started somewhere beyond
the north arch. I could hear the fiddle between shouts.

The puppet booth had a line.

The comic pair were not performing yet. One of them was eating something
from a paper wrapper while the other repaired the bench with a hammer.

Work before work.

We set the Sword board against the rear wall and tied it to an iron ring
meant for something else.

The cheese woman watched.

"That staying?"

"Twenty minutes," Pell said.

"Good."

"Don't like swords?"

"Don't like boards."

"Fair."

Iven put the collection bowl near the edge of the crowd lane.

The loading man appeared from nowhere.

"No."

Iven looked at him.

"Again?"

"Cart wheel."

He pointed.

The bowl sat exactly where a cart turning off the slope would clip it.

Iven moved it beside the rear column.

The cheese woman said, "No."

Iven looked at Teren.

Teren said, "Where?"

She pointed to the corner of her stall.

"Inside that line. People see it. Doesn't block me."

Iven placed it there.

"Thank you."

"Don't lean on cheese."

"I wasn't."

"You look like you might."

Iven stepped away.

First bell after noon was not a single bell.

Three bells sounded within perhaps a minute from different parts of
Dast.

Marek looked at Teren.

"Which?"

Teren said, "Ours."

"Confident."

"No."

He stepped into the lane anyway.

Marek followed.

The King piece began with twelve people watching.

That included two children who had been waiting for cheese.

Marek did not shout immediately.

I noticed because I expected him to.

He walked into the open space with the crown under one arm and said,
conversationally, "I have been informed this is a kingdom."

A man passing with a sack said, "Bad luck."

Marek turned.

"Citizen."

"No."

The man kept walking.

The children laughed.

Marek put on the crown.

The wind took it off.

He caught it against his chest.

More people laughed.

He looked at the crown.

"Rebellion."

That stopped four more.

Serra entered.

The short King piece was mostly theirs. I stayed behind the column with
the Sword board and watched people decide whether we existed.

Some did not.

A woman walked directly through the edge of the scene to buy cheese.

A cart came up the slope.

Marek saw it before I did.

He moved.

Serra moved.

The cart went between them.

The driver said, "Sorry."

Marek said, "Treason."

The driver kept going.

That got a laugh from the cheese woman.

By the time Teren signaled Sword, perhaps thirty people had stopped.

Not thirty still people.

Thirty fair people.

Some eating.

Some carrying bags.

Some looking over shoulders toward somewhere else.

Pell and I brought the board forward.

The rope helped.

The wind still pushed at the mounting cloth.

Nessa had weighted the bottom corners with two small sandbags.

I had not known we owned sandbags.

Apparently we owned everything except money.

Serra mounted me.

The woman selling leeks watched.

"That's him," one child said.

"Who?"

"The sword."

I did not know the child.

That was fine.

Marek began the piece.

A cart bell sounded behind him.

Nobody moved.

The loading man shouted, "Cart!"

Everybody moved.

Including the audience.

For several seconds the performance became a crowd making a lane.

The cart came down the slope loaded with empty grain sacks.

The driver looked at me on the board.

"Sorry."

"You're ruining the kingdom."

"Good."

He passed.

Half the audience returned.

The other half did not.

That was Dast.

Marek resumed.

He did not explain.

Serra picked up from the next useful line.

I answered late because I was watching a strip of mounting cloth trying
to escape the sandbag.

"Pay attention," Serra said in character.

"I am furniture."

"Expensive furniture."

"Then stop leaving me outside."

That worked.

Not huge.

Enough.

The wind pushed my coat against one side of the board.

A boy near the front pointed.

"He's tied."

"I'm mounted."

"Same."

"No."

His mother pulled him back.

"Don't argue with the sword."

"Thank you," I said.

She laughed and put a copper into the bowl.

I saw it.

That was dangerous.

I stopped looking at the bowl.

The Sword ended clean enough.

No goat.

No broken prop.

No accidental jurisdiction.

The crowd was larger than at the beginning and smaller than it had been
halfway through.

That seemed impossible until I looked at the lane.

People were replacing one another.

The widow piece began with Serra seated on the bench and Orin standing
over her with a paper that claimed her dead husband owed him money for
the chair she was sitting on.

The wind took the paper.

Orin watched it go.

Serra said, "Proof?"

He looked toward the lane.

"Traveling."

The paper slapped against a man's boot.

The man picked it up.

Orin held out his hand.

The man read it.

Or pretended to.

"Bad contract."

Serra said, "You hear that?"

Orin said, "He isn't a lawyer."

The man handed it back.

"Neither are you."

Then he left.

The crowd laughed.

Orin looked at Serra.

"I dislike this town."

"Chair's still mine."

"Temporarily."

The piece continued.

It was quieter than Sword.

That helped.

People leaned.

The lane kept moving behind them.

At the end, Serra stood, took the chair, and walked away with it.

Orin stared after her.

"That was collateral."

The applause came unevenly from three sides.

Real enough.

Teren stepped forward.

"Thank you."

Nothing else.

No extra.

Iven stayed beside the bowl while people dispersed.

That mattered.

Copper came after the applause.

Not much.

Then more.

A woman dropped something folded.

A child put in a red berry.

Iven removed the berry.

The child looked offended.

"Money," Iven said.

"It's good."

"Then eat it."

The child took it back and ate it.

We packed before counting.

That was also different now.

Pell untied the board.

I held the rope.

Nessa took the sandbags.

The cheese woman reclaimed her corner before we had fully left it.

"Done?"

"Done," I said.

"Good."

"Thank you."

She handed me a thin slice of cheese.

I stared at it.

"For moving."

I ate it immediately.

At the rear of the arcade, Rinna counted the bowl into her palm.

Teren watched.

I did not.

Marek did.

"Well?"

Rinna kept counting.

"Well?"

"Twenty-six."

Marek's face changed.

"Good?"

"Twenty-six copper," she said.

"I heard the number."

Teren said, "Good enough."

"For?"

"Find Bellan."

Rinna closed her hand over the money.

"Second slot?"

"If it exists."

"Another night?"

"Not yet."

Good.

We found Bellan at the west platform arguing with a man carrying three
drums.

Not the musicians we knew.

Different drums.

Different problem.

Teren waited until Bellan stopped speaking.

"North arcade."

Bellan looked at him.

"Yes."

"Twenty-six."

"Good."

"Cider yard?"

Bellan shook his head.

"Puppets extended."

Marek said, "Sabotage."

Bellan looked at him.

"No."

Teren said, "Then?"

Bellan unfolded a schedule.

"South yard after judging."

"You said mess."

"It is."

"When?"

"Third bell."

"How long?"

"Fifteen."

"Collection?"

"Yes."

"Better traffic?"

"Different."

"Guarantee?"

Bellan looked at him.

Teren said, "I know."

Bellan pointed with the schedule.

"South yard. Fifteen. Don't bring anything you can't clean."

Rinna said, "Today?"

"Today."

Teren looked at her.

She looked back.

"Twenty-six pays part of being here."

"Part?"

"Oats."

"Everything is oats."

"Yes."

Teren turned to us.

"South yard."

Marek smiled.

"We earned mud."

Bellan was already talking to the drummer.

The south yard was worse than mud.

It had been livestock.

The livestock had left.

Evidence remained.

Nessa stood at the edge and said, "No red."

Nobody argued.

The space itself was better.

Open sky.

Temporary rails.

A broad lane between livestock pens and cider sellers.

People had finished judging and were now doing the part of a fair where
they spent money because they were tired of evaluating animals.

Teren cut the bill.

No widow.

No bench.

King and Sword.

Fifteen minutes.

Pell put the collection bowl on an overturned crate where a fair worker
told him it would not be kicked.

The fair worker was right.

Marek was louder this time.

The space needed it.

The first joke died.

The second worked.

A man carrying two cups of cider stopped.

Then three women.

Then a group of boys.

The dog act was performing farther down the lane. I could see the dog
standing upright above shoulders.

They had a crowd too.

Nobody had stolen ours.

The Sword board went on packed dirt instead of stone.

Davin had wedged the rear support before leaving us.

"Don't lean left," Pell told me.

"Why?"

"Ground."

"Helpful."

"You wanted to know."

I did not lean left.

Halfway through, a woman in a green apron shouted, "I saw this
yesterday!"

Marek said, "Impossible."

"At Kest!"

That got my attention.

She pointed at me.

"He was cheaper there!"

I said, "Travel costs."

The crowd laughed.

Marek turned toward me.

"Do not discuss pricing."

"You started a kingdom."

"I didn't start economics."

The woman put a copper in the bowl.

Apparently pricing worked once.

I did not repeat it.

The fifteen minutes went fast.

Not easy.

Fast.

The crowd was larger than north arcade because the lane was broader and
the cider was helping people remain where they were.

It was also worse at listening.

A group talked through Serra.

A man walked between Marek and me carrying a wooden rake.

Two children tried to touch the board.

Pell stopped one.

The other touched my boot.

"Real?"

"Boot?"

"Leg."

"No."

The child looked alarmed.

"Boot is."

His father dragged him away laughing.

At the end, applause mixed with somebody shouting for cider.

Teren thanked them.

Again, no extra.

We packed.

Again, Iven stayed with the bowl.

Again, people paid while leaving.

This time Rinna counted thirty-one copper.

Marek said, "Fifty-seven."

Rinna looked at him.

"I can add."

"Just helping."

"Don't."

Teren said, "Another night?"

Rinna looked toward the wagon field.

"Four for wagons. Horses. Oats. Food."

"Tomorrow crowd?"

"Bigger."

"Work?"

"Not yet."

"Fifty-seven today."

"Gross."

"Yes."

She looked at the copper again.

"One more night."

That was the decision.

Not triumph.

Not disaster.

One more night.

Teren went to find Bellan.

I did not follow.

I went to courier row.

It was not romantic.

It was six tables under a long canvas roof, three clerks, two locked
chests, a wall of destination boards, and a line of people holding
folded paper.

I bought paper, ink use, and carriage west for one copper.

The clerk asked, "Destination?"

"Carrow."

"Name?"

"Lyssa."

"Family?"

I paused.

"No."

He looked at me.

"Where in Carrow?"

"East Market Hall can hold reply."

"That's reply. Where does this go?"

Right.

I gave Lyssa's usual place as carefully as I could.

Then I wrote.

Lyssa,

Still east.

That seemed inadequate.

I crossed it out.

Lyssa,

We reached Dast. It is a harvest fair and everything costs more because
everyone arrived at once. I have now performed beside cheese, livestock,
cider, and a loading slope. The road took longer than I expected.

That was true.

I added:

I am all right. The company is working. I bought two apples at a bridge
and did not share either with Marek.

That seemed more useful.

I stared at the page.

Then:

If you write back, have it held for me at East Market Hall. Teren says
letters usually miss moving companies. This seems like information I
should have asked before leaving.

I almost wrote when I was coming back.

I did not know.

So I wrote:

I miss you.

Then:

Greg

I folded it before I could improve it.

The clerk took the copper and the letter.

"When?"

I asked.

"Carrow?"

"Yes."

"Depends on wagon."

"Helpful."

He put it into a sorting box.

Apparently that was the answer.

When I returned to south three, Rinna had paid for another night.

The S3-41 token was still hanging from the wagon rail.

Davin was feeding the horses.

Nessa was cleaning dirt from the mounting cloth with an expression that
suggested she had personally warned the earth.

Marek was telling Pell that fifty-seven copper proved Dast understood
art.

Rinna said, "Fifty-seven copper proves we paid to stay another night."

"Same."

"No."

Serra sat on the wagon step with the red thread still around her finger.

Orin was asleep under the rear wagon.

Teren had not returned from Bellan.

I touched the inside of my coat.

The brass clasp was still there.

The letter was not.

That felt stranger than it should have.

Pell looked up.

"Where'd you go?"

"Courier."

"Home?"

"Letter."

"Oh."

He went back to cleaning the wooden fish.

No one asked what I wrote.

Dast shouted beyond the field.

Tomorrow would have more people.

Maybe more work.

Maybe more expensive oats.

For tonight, we had paid for our place.

That was enough to stay.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 169

## THE STANDBY

Teren came back after dark with no job.

He also came back with instructions.

"Second bell. West platform."

Rinna looked up from a heel of bread she was cutting into pieces.

"Pay?"

"No."

"Then that's not instructions."

"Bellan says be there."

"Why?"

"Something might break."

Marek, already chewing, said, "Something always breaks."

Rinna pointed the knife at him.

"Not helping."

Teren sat on the wagon tongue.

"The grain speeches are before second bell. Singers after. There's a
half hour in the middle that Bellan says is full."

"Then why are we there?"

"Because he doesn't believe it."

Rinna stared at him.

"Pay?"

"If he uses us, collection. No space fee."

"So Kest again."

"With speeches."

"That's worse."

"Probably."

She cut the last piece of bread.

"We already paid tonight."

"Yes."

"We eat tomorrow whether he uses us or not."

"Yes."

"Horses too."

"Yes."

Rinna handed him bread.

"Then if he doesn't use us by third bell, we stop waiting."

Teren ate.

"Fine."

That was our booking.

Maybe.

The next morning Dast was louder.

I had thought it was loud before.

That had been ignorance.

Market day had expanded while we slept. South Three filled with wagons
before I finished putting on my boot. A family camped two spaces over
had somehow acquired four geese during the night. The geese objected to
this arrangement continuously.

Breakfast was bread, a little cheese, and something Rinna called dried
apple because calling it leather would have reduced morale.

Marek bought a cup of hot milk from a passing woman.

I watched him pay.

He saw me watching.

"Personal expenditure."

"Investment?"

"Breakfast."

"Growth."

"Shut up."

Progress.

Teren wanted only what we could carry to the west platform.

No Sword board.

That surprised me.

"What am I doing?"

"Waiting."

"For?"

"I don't know."

"Useful."

"Very."

He pointed at a small prop basket.

"Carry that."

Apparently I was qualified.

Davin refused to move either wagon.

"Too many."

He meant wagons in the lanes.

Teren looked once at the traffic and agreed.

Pell took a stool. Iven took the collection bowl. Nessa carried two
costume pieces folded inside clean cloth. Serra had already disappeared.

"Where's Serra?" I asked.

Nessa said, "Coming."

That was all I got.

Orin was sitting on the ground lacing one shoe.

His bruise looked better.

The red thread was still around Serra's finger when she returned five
minutes later with a paper cup and no explanation.

Marek said, "Secret?"

She drank.

"No."

"What is it?"

"Tea."

"I meant where were you."

"I know."

We left.

The west platform was not west enough to be quiet.

It stood near a broad intersection between the tool market and the grain
exhibits, raised perhaps three feet on timber supports with steps on
both sides. A cloth roof covered half of it. Benches faced the front,
but the benches did not contain the audience. People stood behind them,
beside them, between carts, near stalls, and on a low wall across the
lane.

A man with a blue sash stopped Teren before we reached the platform.

"You're early."

"Bellan said second bell."

"Second bell hasn't gone."

"That's why we're early."

The man looked at our basket.

"What are you?"

Marek opened his mouth.

Teren said, "Players."

"Scheduled?"

"Standby."

The man made a face that suggested standby was a species of mold.

"Side."

He pointed to a strip of ground behind a canvas partition.

"Don't block the stair. Don't put anything under the platform. Grain
committee uses the rear table."

Teren nodded.

I put the basket beside the canvas.

The man said, "Not there."

I picked it up.

"Where?"

He pointed six feet farther.

"Why?"

"Procession."

"What procession?"

"Grain."

I moved the basket.

Ten minutes later six men carried a painted sheaf of wheat through the
exact place I had been standing.

I stopped asking.

The grain speeches began late.

There were five speakers.

I knew there were five because the blue-sash man counted them twice
while swearing.

The first speaker spoke about yield.

The second spoke about storage.

The third spoke about roads.

The fourth thanked seventeen people.

The fifth was missing.

Bellan appeared at the rear of the platform with a pear.

Different pear, I assumed.

He looked at Teren.

"Ready?"

"For what?"

"Ten."

"Now?"

"After this one."

The fourth speaker was still thanking people.

"Material?" Teren asked.

"Not my problem."

"Collection?"

"Allowed."

"Ten minutes?"

"Nine if he keeps thanking."

Bellan left.

Teren turned.

"Marek. Iven. Serra."

I said, "Me?"

"No."

Good.

Then, "Greg, bowl."

Less good.

Iven handed it to me.

"What do I do?"

"Don't lose it."

"I've done that."

"You lost sight of it."

"Different."

"Today don't do either."

The fifth speaker arrived while the fourth was still thanking people.

The blue-sash man grabbed him by the elbow.

The fifth speaker protested.

The blue-sash man pointed at Bellan somewhere in the crowd.

The fifth speaker stopped protesting.

Teren pulled Marek, Serra, and Iven together.

"King. Debt. Cut after seal."

Iven said, "Which debt?"

"The short one."

Marek said, "Crown?"

"No."

"King without crown?"

"You're still loud."

"Costume is information."

"Then inform them with your face."

Serra finished her tea.

"How long?"

"Nine."

"Eight," the blue-sash man said.

Teren looked at him.

"Eight."

The fourth speaker said, "And finally."

The blue-sash man whispered something obscene.

Teren pointed at the platform.

"Go."

They went.

No rehearsal.

No entrance music.

No board.

No scenery.

Marek walked onto the west platform while the fourth speaker was still
leaving it.

He looked at the benches.

Then at the fifth speaker waiting beside the stairs.

Then at the grain committee table.

"I understand someone here has been promised a turn."

The fifth speaker said, "Yes."

Marek pointed at him.

"Then you understand my problem."

People laughed.

Not many.

Enough to make the fifth speaker look annoyed.

Serra entered from the opposite stair.

Iven followed.

The King piece had been cut so hard I could see the missing parts.

Apparently the audience could not.

Or did not care.

Marek owed Iven money.

Serra claimed the crown had been pledged already.

There was no crown.

Marek used this as evidence that the pledge had been successfully
collected.

Iven said, "Then pay the remainder."

Marek said, "You see? Greed."

The fifth speaker checked the sky.

I stood at the side of the platform with the bowl.

That turned out to be wrong.

People watched from the front.

The bowl was beside me.

No one could reach it without walking around the platform.

I realized this after perhaps two minutes.

I moved toward the front.

The blue-sash man caught my shoulder.

"Not lane."

"I'm collecting."

"Collect there."

He pointed to the low wall across from the platform.

"That's farther."

"That's not lane."

I went.

The wall was better.

People leaving the benches passed it.

I set the bowl on the stone and stood beside it.

A woman dropped in a copper without looking at me.

Then another.

A man put in nothing and said, "Good."

I considered charging him for the word.

The piece ended at perhaps seven minutes.

Teren did not extend.

Marek bowed.

Serra did not.

Iven looked toward me.

I stayed with the bowl.

The fifth speaker climbed the platform.

People shifted.

Some left.

Some stayed for grain.

Copper came from four people.

Then none.

I took the bowl back.

Rinna was not there to count.

Teren poured it into his hand.

"Eleven."

Marek said, "For seven minutes."

"Eight."

"Efficient."

Teren gave the copper to Iven.

"Rinna."

Iven left.

I said, "Now?"

"Wait."

That was the work.

We waited.

The fifth speaker was better than the fourth.

I did not want him to be.

He spoke for six minutes about a grain blight that had apparently ruined
part of the northern crop two years before and what growers had changed
since.

People listened.

Actually listened.

A farmer near me asked another farmer whether he had tried the same
storage method.

The second farmer said it rotted his barley.

They argued quietly.

Nobody cared that we had just performed.

Good.

The singers arrived before the speech ended.

Three women, two men, matching dark green sashes.

They had instruments.

They had cases.

They had someone whose only apparent job was keeping people away from
the cases.

I moved our prop basket farther aside before anyone told me.

Pell noticed.

He said nothing.

I decided that counted.

The singers took the platform.

They were excellent.

Not interestingly excellent.

Annoyingly excellent.

The first song stopped people from the tool lane.

The second filled the benches.

By the third, the low wall where I had put the bowl was occupied by
people listening.

Their collector walked the edge of the crowd with a shallow wooden tray.

He did not wait until the end.

People paid during the song.

I watched him for perhaps thirty seconds.

Then Teren said, "Greg."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"No."

"Good."

He sent me to find Bellan.

That was worse than waiting.

"Where?"

"Ask."

"Who?"

"Anyone who looks angry."

It worked.

A woman at the tool-market gate said Bellan had gone to east judging.

A man at east judging said Bellan had gone to cider.

A cider seller said Bellan had been there ten minutes ago and left
because a rope walker wanted more space.

I found the rope walker first.

She was standing on the ground arguing with two men about a rope that
was not yet in the air.

Bellan stood behind her eating nothing.

Progress.

"Teren wants to know if we're still waiting."

Bellan looked at me.

"Who?"

"East Market."

"The Carrow company."

"East Market."

"Right."

He unfolded a schedule.

"West singers run to third bell."

"I noticed."

"Comic pair lost south corner."

"Why?"

"Pickle seller."

I waited.

"Why?"

"Pickle seller paid for it."

"Fair."

"Comic pair goes east yard after horse prizes. Dog act wants west lane.
Puppets have cider at fourth. You're..."

He looked at the schedule.

Apparently we were nowhere.

"Standby."

"Yes."

"Still?"

"Yes."

"For what?"

"Something breaks."

"Nothing broke."

"Day's young."

He started walking.

I followed.

"Rinna says third bell."

"Who's Rinna?"

"Money."

"Good person to know."

"Very."

He stopped beside a post.

"Tell Teren east yard. After horse prizes. Twelve minutes if comic pair
doesn't take it."

"I thought comic pair was taking it."

"They might not."

"Why?"

"One's sick."

"Which?"

Bellan looked at me.

"I don't know their names."

Fair.

"Pay?"

"Collection."

"Anything else?"

"No."

"Third bell?"

"Before."

"How before?"

"When horses finish."

"When is that?"

"When horses finish."

I hated fairs.

I went back.

Teren listened.

Rinna had returned with Iven.

"Eleven," she said before I could speak.

"East yard," I said. "After horse prizes. Twelve minutes if the comic
pair doesn't take it. One is sick."

"Which?" Marek asked.

"I don't know their names."

"Amateur."

"Collection only," I said.

Rinna looked at Teren.

"Third bell."

Teren nodded.

"If horses finish."

"When?"

"When horses finish."

Rinna closed her eyes.

"Of course."

We moved to east yard.

Not all of us.

Davin stayed with the wagons.

Nessa went back to camp because she refused to carry costume around Dast
for a maybe.

Orin disappeared again after telling Teren he would be at the north food
row.

Teren did not stop him.

Serra left with Nessa, then returned twenty minutes later without the
red thread around her finger.

I noticed.

I did not ask.

The horse prizes took forever.

The horses themselves were beautiful.

I knew this because everyone kept saying so.

Mostly I saw backs, tails, handlers, polished tack, and men standing in
places I wanted to stand.

The east yard had a low judging rail and a patch of open ground beyond
it. Bellan's assistant, not Bellan, told us where to wait.

"Behind the blue rope."

I looked.

There were three blue ropes.

"Which?"

She pointed.

"That one."

"Helpful."

"Don't cross it."

"What happens?"

"Horses."

I stayed behind it.

The comic pair arrived.

Both of them.

Neither looked sick.

Teren looked at them.

They looked at Teren.

One said, "You standby?"

"Yes."

"So are we."

"Thought one of you was sick."

The shorter one pointed at the taller.

"He was."

"I recovered."

"Miracle."

The taller one looked at me.

"Sword?"

"Sometimes."

"Today?"

"I don't know."

"Good fair."

Apparently.

Horse prizes ended.

The crowd did not.

Handlers led animals out through one side. Buyers moved in. Families
pressed toward the rail.

Bellan's assistant spoke to the comic pair.

Then Teren.

Then back to the comic pair.

I could not hear.

Finally she pointed at the platform.

The comic pair went.

Marek said, "We've been betrayed."

Teren said, "No."

"We were promised maybe."

"Exactly."

The comic pair performed the dead goose.

I had seen part of it before.

It was better here.

They used the judging rail as a property line. One claimed the goose had
died on the other's land. The other argued the goose had crossed after
death. A horse handler passing behind them shouted, "Check the feet!"

One of the comics looked at him.

"Expert testimony."

The crowd laughed.

They had ten minutes.

They used ten.

Their collector took a hat through the crowd.

They finished.

The assistant came to Teren.

"Six."

"Minutes?"

"Yes."

Teren looked at us.

"Marek, Greg."

I said, "What?"

"Shopkeeper."

"No Iven?"

"You're collecting from him."

"He's not here."

"You are now collecting from Marek."

Marek said, "I object."

"Good. Use it."

"Six?"

"Five by the time you climb."

There was no climbing for me.

The east yard was level.

For once.

Teren pointed.

"Go."

We went.

Marek entered first.

"I have no money."

I followed.

"Then this will be brief."

That stopped some people who had been turning away after the goose.

Marek put both hands into his empty pockets.

"See?"

"Those are pockets."

"They contain my finances."

"Then your finances owe me money."

A woman laughed.

Marek said, "I am being persecuted for liquidity."

I almost said employment was not evidence.

I felt the line arrive.

I let it die.

"Pay me."

"With what?"

"Those."

I pointed at his boots.

He looked down.

"These are rented."

"Then I know where to send the bill."

A man near the rail said, "Take his coat!"

Marek grabbed his coat closed.

"No."

I said, "Finally, an asset."

The man put a copper into the comic pair's hat.

Their collector was still moving through the edge of the crowd.

I saw it.

So did Marek.

He pointed.

"Wrong creditors."

The comic collector looked at us.

Then at his hat.

Then at our bowl, which Pell had put on the rail.

He took one copper from his hat and dropped it into ours.

The crowd laughed.

I bowed to him.

"Professional courtesy."

He bowed back.

That was the biggest laugh of the piece.

It was not ours.

That was fine.

Teren called, "Done."

We stopped.

Five minutes.

Maybe five and a half.

No ending.

No grand applause.

Marek said, "I remain solvent."

I said, "Temporarily."

Then we were off.

The assistant put another act into the space almost immediately.

A boy with three hoops.

He was better at hoops than I was at anything involving hoops.

Pell took the bowl.

This time we did not leave it behind.

The collection was nine copper.

Twenty for the day.

Not enough to make waiting feel clever.

Not nothing.

Rinna counted it at camp after third bell.

"Twenty."

Teren nodded.

"Yesterday fifty-seven."
